title: MEDuSA
text:
Introduction
Imagine a reinforcement-learning task in which participants decide when to respond and then receive feedback. Choice deliberation varies in duration from trial to trial, while feedback triggers a phasic prediction error. Because hemodynamic responses span 15–30 seconds, BOLD signals evoked by cues, variable-duration decisions, and feedback overlap heavily even when the underlying neural processes are distinct. Depending on the scientific hypothesis, an investigator may want to test:
Michael Hallquist’s 2022 MEDuSA Quant Talk introduced the clock-task motivation for placing deconvolution, event alignment, and multilevel modeling into a unified sequence, while highlighting open methodological challenges around amplitude scaling, temporal resolution, uncertainty propagation, and regional connectivity. This book documents how the standalone medusa R package solves each stage end to end, what assumptions each step makes, and where fundamental identifiability limits remain.

title: MEDuSA
section: Why use MEDuSA—and how does the six-step pipeline fit together?
text:
Why use MEDuSA—and how does the six-step pipeline fit together?
Standard fMRI analysis tools each address part of the problem:

Condition-level task GLMs test prespecified canonical BOLD predictors efficiently, but collapse trial-to-trial variability unless parametric modulators are specified upfront for one model at a time.
Finite impulse response (FIR) models relax HRF shape assumptions for condition averages, but struggle with rapid jittered trial-by-trial modulation and variable reaction-time intervals.
Single-trial GLMs (LSS / LSA) estimate one scalar amplitude per event under an assumed HRF, but do not directly yield a continuous event-locked trajectory across lags or separate cross-fitted vascular timing from continuous background dynamics.
Blind deconvolution (deconvolve_nlreg(), deconvolve_reglin()) reconstructs continuous time series without event timestamps, but suffers from HRF-delay ambiguity, task-contaminated variance scaling, oversmoothing, and lack of an operator-propagated trial error covariance.

MEDuSA combines out-of-sample event-informed neurovascular identification with continuous regularized linear deconvolution and operator-propagated trial inference. Because every linear transformation from raw BOLD to trial readouts is retained explicitly, downstream epoch regressions, parcel aggregations, multilevel models, and connectivity estimators know both the resolution matrix (how neighboring events and lags mix in the mean) and the propagated noise covariance (how observation noise correlates across trials, lags, and parcels).



Pipeline step
Primary medusa function(s)
Core question answered




1. Estimate Cross-Run HRF & Noise
read_nifti_ts(), hrf_library(), estimate_crossrun_hrf()
What HRF shape and AR(\(p\)) noise covariance govern each run and parcel without circularly fitting the target run’s own task amplitudes?


2. Deconvolve Continuous Signal
deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(), diagnose_crossrun_recovery(), write_nifti_ts()
What continuous latent time course is supported on the acquisition grid when event-informed GLS regression anchors noise scaling, adaptive glitch weighting, and GCV smoothing?


3. Align Epochs & De-Mix Overlap
decon_epoch_regression(), align_medusa_ts()
How do we read out event-locked lags, subtract non-target bleed, unmix adjacent target trials, model variable durations, and propagate per-trial standard errors?


4. Assemble Parcel Panels
decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = ...)
How should voxels be precision-weighted into parcels while propagating spatial noise correlations, cohort weights, and ZCA-whitened predictors?


5. Fit Group Multilevel & Trajectory Models
mixed_by(), medusa_multilag_infer(), backproject_medusa()
How do we test planned lag slopes, full multi-lag trajectories, simultaneous bands, and window contrasts across participants?


6. Estimate Connectivity & PPI
decon_connectivity_repair(), medusa_fit_mmom()
How do we disattenuate noisy neural predictors on the right-hand side while accounting for shared regional measurement error?

How to read this book

Read the six step chapters in The six steps. title: Conceptual foundations
text:
Start with the quantity you want to learn
A model of how RPE predicts activity around feedback, an estimate of when a waveform peaks, and a model of how seed activity predicts target activity are three different problems. The first treats recovered activity as a response. The second depends on temporal resolution and the lag family. The third places an estimated variable on the right-hand side, where measurement error can bias the slope. Specify the event, source duration, spatial unit, and scientific contrast before choosing settings.

title: Conceptual foundations
section: The forward model and its inverse
text:
The forward model and its inverse
For one run and voxel, write the measured BOLD vector as
\[
y = H(h)a + Z\gamma + \varepsilon,
\qquad E(\varepsilon)=0,\quad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=\Sigma.
\]
Here \(a\) is activity on the acquisition grid, \(H(h)\) convolves it with the HRF, and \(Z\) contains nuisance terms. Each event can influence many BOLD samples. Two activity patterns with different timing can yield very similar BOLD predictions. A regularized inverse selects among these nearly equivalent patterns using a penalty. In a simplified nuisance-adjusted model,
\[
\widehat a
=\arg\min_a (y-Ha)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(y-Ha)+\lambda\|Pa\|^2.
\]
A larger penalty can suppress noise and broaden or attenuate activity. Smaller penalties can preserve sharper changes and amplify poorly identified directions. The data, forward model, observation mask, and penalty together determine what the estimate resolves. Conditional on fitted settings the inverse is a linear map \(D\). With nuisance handling absorbed into the map, the average recovered signal is \(DH a\). The matrix \(DH\) describes resolution. Its off-diagonal entries describe mixing. Its diagonal entries and lobe integrals describe gain under different source definitions.






Figure 1.1: Two decision intervals of different length and two brief feedback events, with their predicted BOLD contributions. The bottom panel adds those contributions and a temporally correlated error draw.

title: Conceptual foundations
section: Event alignment asks a source question
text:
Event alignment asks a source question
An event-aligned readout is a weighted average of the reconstructed activity around an event. A weight vector answers a question about timing and support. It does not isolate the event’s own contribution if the reconstructed signal contains spillover. The source model makes that contribution explicit. For example, a boxcar with duration equal to RT represents a sustained process. Its height and its integral are different estimands. Report the convention and units, especially when comparing across TRs.
Let \(B\) denote the complete operator from the retained BOLD samples to corrected trial readouts, including centering if relevant. Let \(F\) map the intended source coefficients \(\theta\) into predicted BOLD. Then
\[
\widehat z = B y,
\qquad E(\widehat z\mid B,F) = K\theta,
\qquad K=BF,
\qquad \Omega=\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat z\mid B)=B\Sigma B^\top .
\]
\(K\) and \(\Omega\) answer different questions. \(K\) describes gain and source mixing in the mean. \(\Omega\) describes how measurement error propagates around that mean. A small SE does not tell you whether \(K\) preserves the intended contrast. In medusa, decon_epoch_regression() applies the matched post-demixing resolution operator (\(M_{\text{post}}\)) to centered trial predictors so the regression design and corrected response share compatible coordinates. The same principle governs every transformed panel: identify the linear map and carry both the design and measurement covariance through it.

title: Conceptual foundations
text:
What is independent?

Acquisitions within a run may have serial noise. Retain acquisition indices through censoring. Treating a deleted volume as a shortened clock changes both event design and modeled covariance.
Readouts within a run can share noise because neighboring events and lags use overlapping BOLD data. Run centering induces dependence of its own.
Voxels and parcels can share error. A parcel average can reduce independent noise while leaving common error. A seed and target can show an association from shared motion, vascular signals, nuisance fits, or acquisition noise.
Participants are ordinarily the independent sampling units for population claims. More trials help estimate each participant’s slope. They do not add independent people.

The book uses “activity” for a latent signal under the fitted neurovascular model. Its scale inherits the HRF normalization and input BOLD units. It has no direct calibration to neuronal firing rates.
Keep two kinds of uncertainty in view. Conditional propagation uses fitted HRFs, noise parameters, gains, penalties, and parcel weights as fixed. Sampling uncertainty in a population coefficient also reflects participant variation. For a likelihood or exact finite-sample claim, state the distributional and independence assumptions. Moment propagation itself requires a correct covariance and finite second moments. It does not require Gaussian errors. The M-MOM SE chapter explains how the conditional covariance enters a later model.

title: Conceptual foundations
text:
Decide what to save
Save the event tables and acquisition masks, full subject fits, parcel map, lag grid, behavioral design, and version. Preserve operator summaries and participant identities when combining panels. A CSV can retain trial values and SEs while dropping the attributes used for cross-lag modeling and automatic shared-error correction. The fit objects are the reproducible record. The table is a convenient analysis view.

title: A worked analysis from BOLD to a group claim
text:
Fit the participant and keep the operators
Suppose the primary question is whether signed reward prediction error predicts activity at feedback onset in a prespecified parcel. The teaching dataset has 12 independently simulated participants, three runs each, and 20 trials per run. Each trial contains a cue, a decision interval of variable duration, and brief feedback. Two parcels contain different synthetic voxels. RPE affects feedback activity in both parcels, so the example also shows why a shared task effect must be accounted for in a connectivity analysis.
The simulation source is the package workflow vignette (worked/workflow-source.Rmd), executed directly against library(medusa). The commands below trace the main pipeline handoffs across Steps 1–6; see Reproduction and references to regenerate the checkpoint outputs from scratch.
library(medusa)

hrf_fit <- estimate_crossrun_hrf(
  bold, events, tr, candidates, amplitude_model = "trial",
  noise_model = "ar1", evidence = "calibrated"
)
dec <- deconvolve_crossrun_hrf(
  bold, hrf_fit, lambda = .1, scaling = "noise_sd", penalty = "sobolev",
  nuisance_mode = "ignore", observation_mask = "fit"
)
epochs <- decon_epoch_regression(
  dec, covariates, target_condition = "feedback", lags = -2:4,
  parcel_groups = parcel_ids, restore_scale = TRUE,
  demix_within_trial = FALSE, tau2_mode = "marginal", return_panel = TRUE
)
The fixed penalty is a teaching choice. For a study, check the tuning rule and resolution under the actual timing. Inspect target-excluded training runs and HRF fallbacks. Keep acquisition rows with their original times and explicit validity masks. Verify that every feedback event_index maps to the same row in the behavioral data. Save the named list of participant epoch results so the trajectory and connectivity paths can retrieve their operator metadata.

Fit the planned association
Use a trial-level mixed model with a participant random slope for the within-run predictor and a run intercept nested within participant. Select one parcel and lag before looking at the coefficient.

one <- group_panel[parcel == "Parcel_A" & evt_time == 0]
fit <- mixed_by(
  one, model_formulae = list(
    feedback = decon_demixed ~ rpe_within + (1 + rpe_within || id) + (1 | id:run)
  ),
  weights = "precision_weight_cohort",
  calculate = "parameter_estimates_reml", padjust_by = NULL,
  return_models = TRUE
)

This run retained 720 trial rows and 12 participants in the planned split. The estimated feedback slope was 0.574 in restored input units per RPE unit. The planned mixed model is singular. Inspect the random-effect variance components and report the boundary fit before making a population claim. The checkpoint simulation does not estimate error-rate calibration.

To make the dashed curve, generate only the BOLD contribution from the known feedback RPE effect. title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
text:
3.1 Overview
Before MEDuSA can deconvolve a BOLD time series into latent neural activity, it must know two properties of the observation process: (1) the hemodynamic response function (HRF) that blurs and delays neural events into BOLD fluctuations, and (2) the temporal autocorrelation structure of the scanner and physiological noise. Assuming a single canonical HRF across the brain can shift inferred neural timing by several seconds in fast subcortical or slow association regions, while estimating the HRF on the same run that will later be deconvolved risks tuning the vascular filter to noise or circularly inflating trial effects.
Step 1 (hrf_library() + estimate_crossrun_hrf()) solves this identification problem through leave-one-run-out cross-fitting paired with two-pass post-selection noise estimation. For each target run \(r\), MEDuSA scores a physiologically realistic HRF candidate library exclusively on the participant’s other runs (\(s \neq r\)), pools shape evidence across voxels within functional parcels without averaging raw BOLD signals, and shrinks weak or inconsistent task regions back to a prespecified canonical fallback. Once each target run receives its frozen out-of-sample HRF, MEDuSA refits a stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) noise cascade on run \(r\)’s own task-projected residuals so Step 2 can whiten and invert run \(r\) without circularity or HRF-mismatch bias.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
text:
3.2 Goals of Step 1
Step 1 has four specific estimation goals:

Identify regional HRF timing, width, and undershoot out of sample: Select or smoothly blend candidate HRF shapes for each target run using only training runs (\(s \neq r\)), preventing target-run overfitting.
Prevent noise fitting in silent regions: Require calibrated \(F\)-test task evidence and cross-run compatibility before departing from the canonical HRF; assign silent or erratic regions cleanly to fallback_kernel.
Separate vascular shape from serial noise covariance: Estimate run-specific \(\text{AR}(p)\) autocorrelation parameters (\(\rho, \psi_1, \dots, \psi_4\)) after projecting out nuisance drift, free trial responses, and HRF derivatives under the selected HRF so unmodeled BOLD waves are never mistaken for \(\text{AR}(1)\) persistence.
Record an auditable forward specification: Package the run clocks, valid_rows masks, nuisance designs, training manifests, candidate scores, composite HRF waveforms, and noise parameters into a single crossrun_hrf object so downstream steps never reconstruct timing or masks by guesswork.

What Step 1 deliberately leaves to later steps: Step 1 never sees your behavioral or computational trial covariates (such as reward prediction error or choice value), never modifies the BOLD matrices, and does not produce deconvolved activity or trial slopes. Its trial-amplitude designs exist solely as temporary nuisance/signal subspaces for scoring HRFs and isolating noise residuals.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: 3.3 Inputs: What Step 1 Receives and Why
text:
3.3 Inputs: What Step 1 Receives and Why
Every input to estimate_crossrun_hrf() is structured to preserve exact acquisition timing across runs and censoring gaps:



Input
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




bold
Named list of numeric matrices (time × voxel), one per run (e.g., read_nifti_ts()$bold)
Keeping runs separate (rather than concatenating them) defines the cross-fitting folds (\(s \neq r\)), accommodates unequal run lengths, and prevents AR filters or HRF tails from bleeding across run boundaries. read_nifti_ts() validates shared 3D dimensions, voxel spacing, and sform/qform affines across runs, masks, and atlases before streaming in-mask voxels directly in C++ into matching T × V matrices without materializing 4D R arrays.


events
Named list of data.frames (onset, optional duration, condition) matching names(bold)
HRF shape cannot be identified blindly without anchor timestamps (shifting \(h\) forward and neural timing backward yields identical BOLD). Supplying all modeled task events—without behavioral covariates—anchors vascular lag while keeping behavioral hypotheses blind. Zero-row events[[r]] (e.g., resting-state runs) are permitted and receive canonical fallback HRFs plus pure-nuisance noise fits.


tr & time_offset
Positive scalar TR (s); scalar or per-run start time (s)
Maps continuous event times (in seconds) onto discrete acquisition bins via fractional bracket interpolation or sub-bin boxcar occupancy, ensuring off-TR jitter is represented accurately.


kernel_grid
Numeric matrix (L_hrf × K) from hrf_library(), with column 1 as canonical fallback
Pre-discretizing normalized candidate waveforms onto the tr grid lets C++ evaluate all \(K\) candidates in batched BLAS sweeps and guarantees a known reference shape (fallback_kernel = 1L) when task SNR is absent.


valid_rows
Optional named list of logical vectors (length == nrow(bold[[r]]))
Never delete censored TRs before Step 1. Deleting rows compresses the clock, corrupting causal HRF convolution tails after a scrub gap and pretending separated volumes are lag-1 neighbors. Logical valid_rows keeps the physical time grid intact while excluding bad frames from regression and likelihood scoring.


nuisance
Optional named list of numeric matrices (nrow == nrow(bold[[r]]))
Motion parameters, physiological regressors, or tissue comps supplied here are combined with an automatic run intercept and linear trend so slow scanner drift does not masquerade as broad HRFs or \(\rho \to 1\) autocorrelation.


spatial_groups & noise_groups
Named character/factor vectors mapping voxel_ids to parcels / tissue classes
Separating spatial_groups (functional parcels sharing vascular timing) from optional noise_groups (e.g., tissue/ROI classes sharing serial autocorrelation) lets Step 1 pool low-SNR voxel evidence without averaging raw BOLD series that may carry opposite neural signs.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
section: 3.4 Outputs: What Step 1 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
text:
3.4 Outputs: What Step 1 Produces and Why It Is Set Up That Way
estimate_crossrun_hrf() returns an S3 object of class "crossrun_hrf". Rather than collapsing everything into a single HRF vector per voxel, its components are separated according to their statistical roles in Steps 2–4:



Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way




selected_kernels
Named list (by target run) of L_hrf × voxel matrices
The actual HRF used in Step 2. Storing a per-run, per-voxel matrix allows leave-one-run-out cross-fitting (each run gets the HRF learned on other runs) and represents continuous soft_average composite waveforms that do not correspond to any single column of kernels.


kernel_weights
Named list of K × voxel unit-sum weight matrices
Records the exact Boltzmann + Empirical-Bayes shrinkage weights over library candidates (kernels %*% kernel_weights[[r]], re-normalized under settings$kernel_normalize), making soft composites auditable and reproducible.


selections
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, parcel, kernel_index, status, best_adjusted_partial_r2, selected_task_p, n_compatible_shapes, stability)
Provides human-readable diagnostics and passes out-of-sample task SNR (best_adjusted_partial_r2, selected_task_p) to Step 2 so lambda = NULL tunes deconvolution smoothness only on genuinely task-active units. Note that under soft_average, kernel_index merely names the highest-weight library column—always inspect selected_kernels for the realized shape.


noise
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, group, rho, psi1–psi4, noise_sd, method, n_voxels)
Stores own-run stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) cascade parameters (1 - rho B)(1 - sum psi_j B^j) separately from out-of-sample HRF shapes. Separating noise per run allows scanner autocorrelation to vary across runs while grouping voxels with identical (selected_kernel, ar_vec) into shared linear-operator strata in Steps 2–3.


training_runs & signal_status
Named list of training-run ID vectors; per-run sufficiency table
Explicitly documents cross-fitting provenance (verifying target run \(r\) was excluded from its HRF decision, or recording contiguous sub-block cross-fitting when length(bold) == 1L).


specification & settings
Stored events, nuisance, valid_rows, spatial_groups, tr, kernel_normalize
Freezes the exact forward timing, masks, and normalization convention so deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() and decon_epoch_regression() automatically inherit identical clocks and masks without user book-keeping errors.

title: Step 1: Cross-Run HRF and Noise Estimation
text:
3.5 Recommended Settings

library(medusa)

# 0. Stream preprocessed 4D NIfTI runs + mask + atlas into T x V matrices in C++
ts <- read_nifti_ts(
  niftis = c(run1 = "sub01_run1.nii.gz", run2 = "sub01_run2.nii.gz", run3 = "sub01_run3.nii.gz"),
  mask   = "sub01_mask.nii.gz",
  atlas  = "schaefer200.nii.gz",
  tr     = tr
)
bold <- ts$bold
parcel_ids <- ts$parcel_ids

# 1. Build the 3D physiological HRF manifold (~44 candidates, positive-lobe normalized)
candidates <- hrf_library(tr = tr, preset = "medusa")

# 2. Cross-fit HRF shapes across runs and refit own-run AR(p) noise

text:
3.6 How Step 1 Works in Detail

3.6.1 1. Candidate HRF Library and Positive-Lobe Normalization
Every candidate column \(h_m\) in hrf_library() is evaluated on seq(0, duration, by = tr) as a difference of two gamma densities parameterized by peak delay, dispersion, and positive-to-undershoot ratio (undershoot_ratio = Inf omits the negative dip altogether for fast subcortical/thalamic responses), with the canonical \((6\text{ s}, 1.0, 6)\) curve placed in column 1 as the default fallback.
Under preset = "medusa", kernels use positive-lobe normalization (\(\sum_{t: h_t > 0} h_t = 1\)) rather than signed-sum normalization (\(\sum_t h_t = 1\)). Why? Under signed-sum normalization, a candidate with a deep post-stimulus undershoot has a smaller net sum and is therefore rescaled to a much taller positive peak—artificially shrinking its deconvolved neural amplitude relative to a zero-undershoot candidate! Normalizing by positive-lobe mass keeps unit-impulse neural height comparable across regions with different venous undershoot depths.






Figure 3.1: Three physiological dimensions spanned by hrf_library(..., preset = "medusa") under positive-lobe normalization: peak delay (left), width/dispersion (middle), and post-stimulus undershoot depth including zero-undershoot subcortical shapes (right).



Because observed BOLD convolves neural events with the local vascular filter, identical neural event trains produce shifted and broadened BOLD peaks in fast versus slow vascular territories (Figure 3.2). Step 1 learns that territory-specific filter before deconvolution begins.






Figure 3.2: Simulated neural event amplitudes (top) and resulting noisy BOLD signals in a fast-HRF versus slow-HRF parcel (bottom) from the Step 1 demonstration (TR = 0.65 s).





3.6.2 2. Leave-One-Run-Out Cross-Fitting (and Single-Run Block Splitting)
For target run \(r\) in a multi-run session (\(R \ge 2\)), candidate HRF scores are computed exclusively on runs \(s \neq r\), while run \(r\)’s own data are used only after HRF selection to estimate run \(r\)’s noise covariance (Figure 3.3). Perturbing bold$run1 arbitrarily leaves hrf_fit$kernel_weights$run1 and hrf_fit$selected_kernels$run1 unchanged to machine precision (0 in Figure 3.4).
What if a participant has only one task run (length(bold) == 1L)? Rather than failing or fitting in-sample, estimate_crossrun_hrf() automatically partitions usable observations into contiguous temporal sub-blocks (3 blocks when \(n_{\text{valid}} \ge 120\), 2 halves when \(40 \le n_{\text{valid}} < 120\)), scores candidates on each sub-block against the full causal event design (preserving HRF tails across block boundaries), tests cross-block shape compatibility, and returns a single continuous HRF for the intact run.






Figure 3.3: Cross-fitting separation in a three-run dataset: candidate HRF evidence for target run \(r\) comes strictly from runs \(s \neq r\), while serial noise parameters are refit on run \(r\) itself.









Figure 3.4: Invariance verification: adding strong synthetic oscillations to target Run 1 leaves its cross-fitted HRF candidate weights completely unchanged.





3.6.3 3. Calibrated Evidence Scoring, Amplitude Models, and Spatial Pooling
Within each training run \(s \neq r\), MEDuSA whitens the usable rows under a first-pass noise filter, projects out the nuisance subspace \(Z_s\), and measures how much residual variance each candidate HRF explains via degree-of-freedom-adjusted partial \(R^2\), accompanied by an effective-DF Satterthwaite \(F\)-test (selected_task_p).
Two design choices govern whether training runs detect genuine neural signal:

Condition-mean vs. trial-wise training designs (amplitude_model): When trial responses fluctuate symmetrically around zero (such as a zero-mean reward prediction error), a single condition-mean regressor cancels positive and negative trials and misses the HRF completely (Figure 3.6). Setting amplitude_model = "trial" frees per-event amplitudes (evaluating one condition freed at a time in multi-condition schedules) so unsigned trial variance identifies the vascular shape—still without touching external behavioral predictors.
Parcel evidence pooling (pooling = "parcel"): Pooling averages precision-weighted candidate score profiles across voxels in a parcel after squaring voxelwise \(t\)/\(R^2\) evidence, so voxels with opposite-signed task effects reinforce rather than cancel one another (Figure 3.5, Figure 3.7). Regions without calibrated task support (Null in Figure 3.5) fail the departure gate and fall back cleanly to hrf_1.







Figure 3.5: Out-of-sample adjusted partial \(R^2\) surfaces for target Run 1 across the 27-candidate cortical slice (Fast truth: \(4.5\text{ s}, 0.9\); Slow truth: \(7.5\text{ s}, 1.1\); Null: pure \(\text{AR}(3)\) noise). Crosses mark generating parameters.









Figure 3.6: Zero-mean alternating trial amplitudes (amplitude_model = "condition" vs. "trial"): freeing trial amplitudes recovers the true \(7.5\text{ s}\) HRF where a condition-mean regressor collapses to canonical fallback.









Figure 3.7: Voxelwise hard selection vs. parcel-pooled selection across heterogeneous voxel noise levels (0.012 to 0.055). Parcel pooling eliminates noisy single-voxel jumps.



Under selection_mode = "soft_average", compatible library candidates are combined via Boltzmann weights scaled by cross-run noise SE and shrunk toward column 1 by Empirical-Bayes departure confidence (Figure 3.8).






Figure 3.8: Generating HRFs, hard-selected library nodes, and soft_average composite HRFs for the Fast and Slow parcels in Run 1.

3.6.4 4. Two-Pass Post-Selection \(\text{AR}(p)\) Noise Refitting
In fMRI, task-evoked BOLD responses are smooth low-frequency waves. If noise autocorrelation is estimated under a misspecified canonical HRF (for instance, a \(6.0\text{ s}\) filter applied to a \(4.5\text{ s}\) Fast region), unmodeled task-timing residuals leak into the error series and bias \(\hat{\rho}\) upward toward the stationarity boundary!
To prevent HRF mismatch from corrupting the whitener, estimate_crossrun_hrf() performs a post-selection two-pass REML noise refit on each run \(r\):

Using the cross-fitted HRF \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\), hrf_build_noise_mean_design() constructs a rich nuisance-and-task projection subspace containing run intercept/trend, user nuisance, DF-adaptive \(<1/128\text{ Hz}\) DCT cosines, convolved free-trial columns, and 1st/2nd condition HRF Taylor derivatives (degrading gracefully when residual degrees of freedom are tight).
Within contiguous unmasked segments of valid_rows[[r]], MEDuSA pools bias-corrected profile REML across group voxels to select \(\hat{\rho} \in [-0.8, 0.9]\) and fits up to \(q \le 4\) higher-order innovation-whitened Yule–Walker parameters \((\psi_1, \dots, \psi_q)\) representing \((1 - \rho B)(1 - \sum_{j=1}^q \psi_j B^j)\varepsilon_t = u_t\), followed by a second GLS pass so task projection itself uses the learned covariance.

In our TR = 0.65 s simulation with true \(\text{AR}(3)\) parameters \((\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30)\), refitting noise under the cross-fitted HRF recovers virtually identical cascade parameters across Fast, Slow, and Null parcels (Table 3.2) and flattens true error autocorrelation across all lags (Figure 3.9)—whereas a misspecified fixed canonical HRF distorts the Fast parcel’s whitener. See the Woolrich autocorrelation assessment for a side-by-side comparison against FILM-style Tukey tapers.

3.7 Diagnostic Checklist Before Proceeding to Step 2

Verify target-run exclusion: Check hrf_fit$training_runs to confirm every run’s HRF was trained strictly on \(s \neq r\) (or sub-block cross-fit if \(R = 1\)) and inspect hrf_fit$signal_status for dropped or zero-event runs.
Inspect realized composite waveforms, not just kernel_index: Plot hrf_fit$selected_kernels for key parcels to check physiological plausibility and fallback rates (status == "fallback_prespecified").
Audit hrf_fit$noise: Check for widespread boundary hits (rho == 0.90 or -0.80), which usually signal unmodeled drift, motion spikes, or unrecorded task events missing from events or nuisance.



Mathematical Details & Edge-Case Rules


Cross-fitted evidence pooling: For candidate \(m\) on training run \(s \neq r\), whitened nuisance-orthogonalized BOLD \(y_{s,\perp}\) is regressed onto whitened candidate design \(X_{s,m,\perp}\) (rank \(d_{s,m}\) over \(n_s\) valid rows), yielding adjusted partial \(R^2_{s,m} = 1 - (1 - R^2_{s,m})\frac{n_s - p_Z}{n_s - p_Z - d_{s,m}}\). Across training runs, scores are weighted by effective degrees of freedom and checked for sign/peak compatibility (stability).
Soft-average shrinkage: Compatible candidates within score_margin receive Boltzmann weights \(w_m \propto \exp(\Delta R^2_m / \tau_{\text{SE}})\) blended with column 1 ((1 - \eta) e_1 + \eta w), where Empirical-Bayes shrinkage \(\eta \in [0, 1]\) approaches 0 as calibrated task \(F\)-statistics weaken toward the evidence_alpha threshold.
Exact gapped covariance: When valid_rows[[r]] masks interior frames, AR estimation restricts lag products strictly within contiguous unmasked runs of frames, while Step 2’s whitener \(W_r\) inverts the exact stationary Toeplitz submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\) on retained timestamps \(I_r\) so multi-TR scrub gaps decay correlation by \(\gamma(|t_a - t_b|)\) rather than treating across-gap neighbors as 1 TR apart.

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
text:
4.1 Overview
Once Step 1 has learned each run’s out-of-sample HRF and serial noise structure, Step 2 (deconvolve_crossrun_hrf()) reconstructs a continuous latent neural activity time series \(\hat{s}(t)\) on the original acquisition grid for every run and voxel. Because hemodynamic convolution acts as a sluggish low-pass filter, directly inverting \(H(h)\) amplifies high-frequency scanner noise violently; conversely, over-penalizing smoothness blurs rapid cognitive transitions and shrinks trial peaks.
What makes MEDuSA’s Step 2 fundamentally stronger than traditional blind deconvolution (deconvolve_nlreg(), deconvolve_reglin())—while remaining far more flexible than a rigid parametric GLM—is its hybrid event-informed continuous architecture. The deconvolved signal \(\hat{s}(t)\) itself is estimated continuously and unconstrained across the entire run (never clamped to zero outside events or restricted to fixed trial boxcars). Simultaneously, MEDuSA uses an auxiliary event-informed GLS regression model under the hood to separate evoked task BOLD from background noise—anchoring pure observation-noise scaling (scaling = "noise_sd"), protecting genuine neural bursts during adaptive artifact downweighting (rwls = "auto"), tuning smoothness on task-active regions (lambda = NULL), and exporting the exact linear inverse operator needed by Step 3 to de-mix overlapping epochs and propagate standard errors.

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
text:
4.2 Goals of Step 2
Step 2 addresses five tightly linked goals:

Estimate continuous, unconstrained latent neural dynamics: Recover a continuous time-by-voxel activity matrix \(\hat{s}_r\) on the full \(n_r\)-sample acquisition grid via AR(\(p\))-whitened, smoothness-penalized generalized least squares (GLS).
Place voxels and runs on an uncontaminated noise-SD reference scale: Isolate marginal observation-noise standard deviation (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)) from task-evoked BOLD variance via event-informed GLS residuals (scaling = "noise_sd"), avoiding the signal-induced compression of whole-run zscore scaling.
Suppress sub-scrubbing scanner glitches without clipping heavy neural responses: Downweight transient motion or RF artifacts orthogonal to the task-HRF subspace (rwls = "auto") while protecting genuine high-amplitude neural bursts and HRF latency shifts.
Tune regularization (lambda) for downstream trial inference rather than raw BOLD prediction: Balance prewhitened generalized cross-validation (GCV) against gain-restored trial variance and modulation transfer across task-supported voxels.
Preserve the complete linear operator state for Step 3–6 handoffs: Retain the exact HRF/noise strata, scaling divisors, task-free whitened noise_innovations, and frame_weights so downstream epoch de-mixing, parcel SEs, and connectivity models propagate exact covariances.

What Step 2 deliberately leaves to Step 3: Continuous regularized deconvolution cannot simultaneously achieve low noise and zero event cross-talk—every finite \(\lambda > 0\) leaves known amplitude shrinkage (\(R_{ii} < 1\)) and local temporal spread (\(R_{ij} \neq 0\)) in decon$activity. Step 2 leaves raw activity un-inflated and hands the exact linear operator to decon_epoch_regression() (Step 3) to de-mix overlapping events and restore amplitude gain at the trial-epoch level.

title: Step 2: Event-Informed Continuous Deconvolution
section: 4.3 How Event-Informed Regression Works—and Why It Improves Over Blind Deconvolution
text:
4.3 How Event-Informed Regression Works—and Why It Improves Over Blind Deconvolution
A recurring question for fMRI researchers is: Why does MEDuSA use event timestamps during deconvolution instead of performing purely blind deconvolution, and if it uses event timestamps, why isn’t it just an ordinary task GLM? Understanding this distinction is the key to understanding Step 2.

4.3.1 Why Blind Deconvolution Struggles on Event-Related fMRI
Blind deconvolution algorithms—such as Bush & Cisler’s (2011) nonlinear sigmoid encoding (deconvolve_nlreg() / algorithm = "bush2011") or blind linear ridge/spline deconvolution (deconvolve_reglin())—receive only a raw BOLD vector \(y\) and a fixed canonical kernel \(h\), with no knowledge of when task events occurred. That blindness creates four compounding distortions:

Shift-shape unidentifiability and latency inversion: Convolving a delayed neural spike with a fast HRF produces the exact same BOLD peak as convolving an early neural spike with a slow HRF. Without cross-run event regression (Step 1), blind deconvolution locks onto a single assumed HRF, shifting inferred neural onset times backward or forward whenever regional vasculature differs from canonical.
Task-contaminated amplitude scaling (zscore) and nonlinear ceiling compression: Because blind methods cannot separate evoked BOLD signal from background noise, they standardize each voxel by its total whole-run BOLD SD (zscore). In strongly task-responsive voxels, evoked BOLD variance inflates the denominator \(\text{SD}(y)\), shrinking recovered neural slopes relative to noisier or weaker voxels! Worse, Bush’s nonlinear algorithm passes latent encoding through a logistic sigmoid \(\hat{e}_t = (1 + e^{-x_t})^{-1} \in (0, 1)\), compressing heavy-tailed neural bursts against an artificial upper ceiling and destroying linear superposition.
Oversmoothed GCV and unguarded outlier trade-offs: Blind GCV averages prediction error across all brain voxels—including silent white-matter/null voxels where optimal \(\lambda = \infty\)—dragging the global penalty toward oversmoothing. Meanwhile, any attempt at blind outlier downweighting treats a genuine \(4\times\) neural prediction-error burst and a scanner spike identically because both produce large BOLD excursions.
No task-free noise innovations or linear operator covariance: Blind outputs provide only a point-estimate time series, leaving downstream trial regressions with no analytical per-trial se_demixed, no cross-trial resolution matrix, and task-contaminated spatial noise correlations.



4.3.2 How MEDuSA’s Hybrid Event-Informed Architecture Works
MEDuSA separates what is constrained from what is informed by events:

The latent activity trajectory \(\hat{s}_r\) itself is continuous and unconstrained. Given scaled, centered usable observations \(\tilde{y}_{r,o}\), the Step 2 solver minimizes the penalized prewhitened GLS objective over \(\mathbb{R}^{n_r}\): \[
\hat{s}_r = \arg\min_{s \in \mathbb{R}^{n_r}} \left\| W_r \bigl(\tilde{y}_{r,o} - M_{r,o} H_r s\bigr) \right\|_2^2 + \lambda s^\top P s
\] Notice that event timestamps do not appear inside the penalty \(P\) or constrain \(s\). Spontaneous inter-trial fluctuations, sustained deliberation plateaus, and unmodeled temporal profiles are free to emerge anywhere on the acquisition grid.
Event-informed GLS regression (hrf_build_noise_mean_design()) anchors the four calibration quantities surrounding that continuous solve:

Uncontaminated marginal noise scaling (scaling = "noise_sd"): Before inverting \(H_r\), hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd() builds an event-informed design matrix \(X_{\text{ev}}\) containing run intercept/trend, user nuisance, \(<1/128\text{ Hz}\) DCT drift cosines, free per-trial convolved event columns under \(\hat{h}^{(-r)}\), and 1st/2nd condition HRF Taylor derivatives (absorbing trial-to-trial latency jitter). Projecting \(X_{\text{ev}}\) out in unit-marginal AR(\(p\))-whitened space (\(e = (I - Q Q^\top) W_{\text{unit}} y\)), dividing by GLS leverage \(\sqrt{1 - h_{tt}}\), and Winsorizing at \(3 s_{\text{MAD}}\) isolates pure observation noise \(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{marg}}\)—completely invariant to how strongly a voxel responds to the task—and saves the orthonormalized task-free noise_innovations for Step 4 parcel SEs and Step 6 connectivity!
Task-envelope-guarded adaptive glitch weighting (rwls = "auto"): Real fMRI runs contain sub-scrubbing motion micro-jerks and RF spikes (\(\text{FD} \approx 0.2\text{--}0.4\text{ mm}\)) that ring through a linear inverse filter. hrf_estimate_rwls_weights() evaluates cross-voxel residual energy orthogonal to the [trial HRF, dHRF/dt] subspace and expands frame tolerance proportionally to the convolved task-design envelope. If a run passes a Winsorized-SVD Liu–Tang–Zhang (2009) spatial null gate (\(p < 0.01/m\)), MEDuSA downweights genuine non-task scanner glitches—routing isolated impulses to rank-\(k\) Woodbury Sparse Bayesian Learning (\(\Sigma_{\text{AR}} + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\), preventing AR(\(p\)) whitening smearing!) and sustained physiological bursts to innovation-space rWLS—while keeping \(w_t = 1.0\) on heavy neural bursts!
Task-SNR-weighted, gain-calibrated GCV (lambda = NULL): hrf_tune_decon_lambda() restricts tuning to voxels with positive out-of-sample task \(R^2\) from Step 1 (selections), pooling across all usable runs in an order-invariant pass and trading prewhitened GCV fit against Stage-3 gain-restored trial level/contrast variance and modulation transfer.
Exact linear operator handoff (D_r): Because \(\hat{s}_r = D_r \tilde{y}_{r,o}\) remains strictly linear conditional on its weights, Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) can pass the event schedule forward through \(D_r H_r\) to de-mix overlapping cues/targets and propagate exact per-trial SEs.

Output Component
Structure
Why It Is Set Up That Way

Named list of n_time × n_voxels matrices (with tr, time_offset, observation_mask attributes)
Preserves the full original acquisition grid even when interior frames were censored (valid_rows = FALSE), so event lag clocks never shift and continuous visual diagnostics remain aligned to run seconds. Invalid/zero-variance voxels receive NA columns rather than crashing the batch.


scaling
Named list of per-run data.frames (voxel, center, scale, noise_sd, status)
Records both the applied pre-deconvolution divisor (scale) and the estimated marginal observation-noise SD (noise_sd). Separating scale from noise_sd allows Step 3 to multiply activity back into physical BOLD units (restore_scale = TRUE) while still propagating exact observation-noise SEs!

Named list of n_valid_rows × n_voxels unit-norm task-free whitened residual matrices
Extracted from hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd() after projecting out free-trial task responses and HRF derivatives. Allows Step 4 to compute uncontaminated within-parcel spatial noise variance and Step 6 to estimate cross-parcel shared-error correlations (shared_noise_loading).

Named list of length-n_valid_rows numeric vectors in \((0, 1]\) (with attr(, "weight_space"))
Records the realized rwls weights per run (1 everywhere when clean). Passing frame_weights forward ensures diagnose_crossrun_recovery() and decon_epoch_regression() reconstruct the exact weighted inverse operator \(D_r(w_r)\) and Woodbury/innovation noise covariance!

Embedded crossrun_hrf object + resolved inverse settings (including lambda and lambda_tuning)
Avoids storing gigabytes of dense \(n_r \times m_r\) inverse matrices in RAM: because voxels are grouped into (HRF, AR) strata, Step 3 can rebuild each unique stratum operator \(D_r\) on the fly in milliseconds using hrf_fit, settings, and frame_weights.

4.7 Core Deconvolution Mechanisms & Sensitivity Checks

4.7.1 1. Why Regularization Is Unavoidable—and How Penalties Shape \(\hat{s}(t)\)
Because the HRF smooths over 15–30 seconds, adding a rapid \(+1/-1\) oscillation to neural activity changes predicted BOLD almost imperceptibly (Figure 4.2). An unpenalized or weakly penalized inverse (lambda = 0.0001) explodes high-frequency noise, whereas heavy regularization (lambda = 3) over-smooths and shrinks peaks (Figure 4.3).






Figure 4.2: High-frequency forward ambiguity: adding rapid alternating neural fluctuations produces virtually identical convolved BOLD.









Figure 4.3: Effect of varying lambda (0.0001, 0.03, 3) on the same noisy BOLD series under the sobolev penalty.



Comparing all five quadratic penalties (ridge, diff1, diff2, matern1, sobolev) under automatic tuning (Figure 4.4, Table 4.3) shows why sobolev and matern1 provide a stable middle ground: pure diff2 leaves global linear trends unpenalized (RMSE = 0.390 vs. 0.264 for sobolev), while pure ridge pulls every sample independently toward zero without sharing smoothness across adjacent TRs.

4.7.2 2. Adaptive Multi-Run GCV Tuning (lambda = NULL)
Standard observation-space GCV minimizes BOLD prediction error, which favors stronger smoothing than optimal for estimating sharp trial contrasts. MEDuSA’s hrf_tune_decon_lambda() (Figure 4.5) evaluates each grid candidate across active voxels/runs and combines prewhitened GCV with Stage-3 gain-restored level variance (var_level), 1-TR contrast variance (var_contrast), and modulation transfer (mtf_rel) weighted by Step 1’s task SNR.






Figure 4.5: Comparison of raw prewhitened GCV versus MEDuSA’s adaptive task-weighted criterion (top) and the underlying gain-restored level and contrast variance proxies (bottom).





4.7.3 3. Resolution, Leakage, and diagnose_crossrun_recovery()
Even with known HRF and optimal \(\lambda\), the resolution matrix \(R = D H\) is not the identity matrix. Dividing a single point readout by its diagonal gain \(R_{tt}\) restores isolated peak height to 1, but simultaneously amplifies off-peak side lobes and noise (Figure 4.6) and leaves directed event-to-event cross-talk across closely spaced trials (Figure 4.7). diagnose_crossrun_recovery(decon) quantifies both self-gain (mean_gain = 0.549 in Run 1, 0.637 in Run 2) and neighbor leakage (mean_abs_excess_leakage ≈ 0.021–0.024) on your exact event schedule before Step 3 performs matrix de-mixing.






Figure 4.6: Impulse resolution curves \(R_{:,91}\) at weak, moderate, and strong \(\lambda\): raw recovery (top) versus scalar division by diagonal gain (bottom).









Figure 4.7: Event-by-event normalized excess cross-talk matrix from diagnose_crossrun_recovery() across 15 Run 1 events.





4.7.4 4. Nuisance Handling, Observation Masks, Scaling, and Boundaries
Finally, Figure 4.8, Figure 4.9, and Figure 4.10 illustrate four operational rules to verify in every dataset:

Nuisance consistency (Figure 4.8, top): When low-frequency drift remains in bold, nuisance_mode = "ignore" lets that drift pass directly into activity; use nuisance_mode = "joint" unless bold was already detrended upstream.
Observation masks (Figure 4.8, bottom): Setting valid_rows = FALSE across an artifact window (70–80 s) with observation_mask = "fit" bridges the gap smoothly using the penalty and surrounding causal BOLD support without letting the spike corrupt neighboring trials—though interpolated values inside a long gap are prior-driven, not observed data (Step 3 will automatically gate poorly supported trial-lags to NA).
Scaling restoration (Figure 4.9): Multiplying scales$noise_sd$activity or scales$zscore$activity by scaling[[r]]$scale reproduces demean activity to < 1e-8 (3.11e-15 in verification.txt), while noise_sd tracks true \(\sigma\) cleanly across heterogeneous voxels.
Run-end boundaries and HRF delay sensitivity (Figure 4.10): Appending artificial zero BOLD observations (tail_padding = 33L) pulls valid late-run activity downward, while a \(+2\text{ s}\) HRF delay error shifts inferred neural peaks ~2 s earlier—underscoring why Step 1’s cross-run HRF learning and tail_padding = 0L are essential.







Figure 4.8: Joint vs. ignored nuisance handling (top) and masked vs. unmasked artifact window 70–80 s (bottom).









Figure 4.9: Comparison of whole-run BOLD SD (zscore), event-informed GLS noise_sd, and true generating observation-noise SD across 8 voxels.









Figure 4.10: Sensitivity to run-end zero padding (tail_padding = 33L vs. 0L, top) and a 2-second HRF delay misspecification (bottom).





Mathematical Reference: Weighted GLS Operator & Woodbury SBL

Let \(I_r \subset \{1, \dots, n_r\}\) index the \(m_r\) valid rows (valid_rows[[r]] == TRUE), \(M_{r,o}\) select rows \(I_r\), \(H_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n_r \times n_r}\) be the causal Toeplitz HRF convolution matrix for stratum kernel \(h\), and \(Z_{r,o}\) be the active nuisance basis ([1, trend, nuisance] under nuisance_mode = "joint", empty under "ignore").

Exact gapped whitening & nuisance projection: \(W_r = L_r^{-1}\) is the inverse Cholesky factor of the exact stationary \(\text{AR}(p)\) correlation submatrix \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r]\). Under rwls_space = "woodbury" with transient variances \(\delta_t^2 = (1 - w_t)/w_t\) on flagged frames \(S\), MEDuSA whitens against \(\Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] + \operatorname{diag}(\delta^2)\) via a rank-\(|S|\) Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury update in \(O(m_r |S|)\) operations, preventing high-\(\rho\) AR filters from smearing an isolated glitch into adjacent clean frames. Orthogonalizing \(Q_Z = \operatorname{orth}(W_r Z_{r,o})\) projects out nuisance terms jointly via \(\tilde{W}_r = (I - Q_Z Q_Z^\top) W_r\).
Linear inverse operator: With \(A_r = \tilde{W}_r M_{r,o} H_r\) and penalty \(P_{\lambda} = \lambda P + \epsilon_{\text{ridge}} I_{n_r}\), the frozen inverse operator is \[
D_r = \bigl(A_r^\top A_r + P_{\lambda}\bigr)^{-1} A_r^\top \tilde{W}_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n_r \times m_r},
\] evaluated across voxel batches via Cholesky solves in C++ (backend = "cpp", agreeing with backend = "r" to 2.71e-14).

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
text:
5.1 Overview
Deconvolving a BOLD run in Step 2 produces a continuous time series \(\hat{s}_r\) on the acquisition clock—not isolated single-trial numbers. Simply slicing or linearly interpolating \(\hat{s}_r\) around each event onset (the legacy alignment route) leaves two systematic distortions: (1) regularization shrinkage, which attenuates true trial amplitudes (\(g_i < 1\)), and (2) cross-event mixing, where preceding cues, motor responses, or rapid neighboring trials bleed through the regularized inverse operator \(D_r H_r\) into the target readout. Moreover, when an event represents a variable-duration deliberation interval (such as reaction time), a fixed-point readout conflates firing rate with time-on-task.
Step 3 (decon_epoch_regression()) bridges continuous deconvolution and trial-level modeling by passing the forward event schedule through the exact frozen Step 2 inverse operator. For every requested lag \(\tau\) around target_condition, it integrates local continuous activity via symmetric kernel quadrature, subtracts operator-predicted bleed from non-target events (demix_other_events = TRUE), inverts the target-by-target resolution matrix to remove neighbor cross-talk and restore amplitude gain (demix_target_trials = TRUE), aligns centered trial covariates through the matched post-demixing operator (\(M_{\text{post}}\)), and propagates Step 1–2’s \(\text{AR}(p)\) observation-noise covariance through the entire composite linear map \(B_{r,\tau}\) to deliver exact conditional per-trial standard errors (se_demixed), Empirical-Bayes precision weights, and within-run ZCA-whitened variables.

title: Step 3: Epoch Alignment, De-Mixing, and Uncertainty Propagation
text:
5.2 Goals of Step 3
Step 3 accomplishes five core objectives:

Read out event-locked lag trajectories without mutating the acquisition clock: Sample continuous activity around each target onset \(t_i + \tau\) using jitter-tolerant quadrature (readout_kernel) while gating out trial-lags that lack causal unmasked BOLD support (obs_frac_tau < 0.20).
De-mix interfering events and adjacent target trials: Use the stratum resolution operator \(D_r H_r\) to subtract preceding/succeeding non-target event bleed (e.g., cues) and invert target-to-target cross-talk while restoring regularization-attenuated amplitude gain.
Define duration-explicit neural estimands when intervals vary: Support impulse ("impulse"), fixed-window ("window"), and RT-matched sustained boxcar ("duration") forward models, distinguishing constant firing rate (duration_scale = "rate", baseline-deconfounded from RT) from integrated neural mass ("integral").
Keep predictors and responses in matched operator coordinates: Transform centered within-run predictors by the post-demixing resolution operator \(M_{\text{post}}\) so residual ridge shrinkage at short ISIs never biases trial regression slopes.
Propagate observation-noise covariance analytically to the trial level: Compute conditional per-trial measurement SEs (se_demixed), lag-1 trial error autocorrelation (error_ac1), Empirical-Bayes trial precision weights, and regularized within-run ZCA whitening matrices without Monte Carlo resampling.

What Step 3 deliberately leaves to Steps 4–6: Step 3 operates within a single participant’s multi-run fit. Combining voxels into parcels is covered in Step 4 (which runs inside the same decon_epoch_regression() call via parcel_groups), population inference across participants is handled in Step 5, and disattenuating noisy seed predictors is handled in Step 6.






TipDescriptive Event Alignment (align_medusa_ts()) vs. Operator De-Mixing (decon_epoch_regression())



When you want descriptive event-locked interpolation and overlap/censoring auditing without assuming a forward event design—for example, plotting raw peri-event BOLD waveforms, inspecting blind deconvolve_nlreg() / deconvolve_reglin() trajectories, or running sensitivity checks under explicit overlap_policy = "allow" | "truncate" | "exclude"—use align_medusa_ts() (or evt_align_decon_files() for disk-backed .csv.gz / .rds archives). align_medusa_ts() runs directly on T × V matrices, "medusa_nifti_ts" bundles (read_nifti_ts()), or deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() outputs in C++ using the same four readout kernels ("linear", "boxcar", "triangle", "gaussian"), gap-fencing (max_gap), censoring (valid = "observation_mask"), and epoch_status / source_clock provenance without expanding long fmri_ts tables. For primary inferential modeling on deconvolve_crossrun_hrf() fits, prefer decon_epoch_regression(), which retains the Step 2 inverse operator \(D_r\) to remove non-target bleed, unmix adjacent target trials, restore regularization gain, and propagate exact analytical se_demixed and precision_weight_cohort.

5.6 Step 3 Mechanisms Illustrated

5.6.1 1. Kernel Quadrature Readouts and Causal BOLD Support Gating
At each target onset \(t_i\) and lag \(\tau\), build_epoch_readout_matrix() constructs a row-normalized weight vector \(S_\tau[i, :]\) over the discrete acquisition grid (Figure 5.1). "linear" uses 2-point bracket interpolation, whereas "triangle" (default, width \(1.5 \times \text{TR}\)), "boxcar", and "gaussian" integrate 9-point symmetric quadrature nodes across adjacent TRs—attenuating high-frequency deconvolution noise while honoring exact sub-TR event jitter.
Crucially, MEDuSA checks causal BOLD observability (obs_frac_tau >= 0.20): if at least 80% of the forward HRF energy evoked by a source at \(t_i + \tau\) falls inside censored frames (valid_rows == FALSE) or past the end of the run, decon_epoch_regression() marks that trial-lag NA rather than fabricating a number from smoothness prior extrapolation!






Figure 5.1: Acquisition-grid readout weights around an off-grid target timestamp (20.35 s, TR = 1 s) for "linear", "boxcar", "triangle", and "gaussian" kernels.





5.6.2 2. Non-Target Subtraction (demix_other_events) & Target De-Mixing (demix_target_trials)
Consider a cue–feedback paradigm (Cue followed 1–3 s later by Feedback) with three simulated voxels (simulate_step3.R): Cue_only (responds to cues with zero feedback effect), Target (true feedback slope 0.70 on x), and Noisy_target (true slope 0.70, higher noise). Because RT links cue-to-feedback delay with x, uncorrected feedback readouts in Cue_only pick up spurious cue bleed (beta_raw = -0.115), while Target is severely attenuated (beta_raw = 0.088 vs. truth 0.700; Table 5.1, Figure 5.3).

Target de-mixing alone (target_only) restores gain on target overlap (0.307) but magnifies unsubtracted cue bleed in Cue_only (-0.401).
Cue + target de-mixing (default, demix_ridge = 0.05) removes constant-amplitude cue bleed (Cue_only slope -0.006) and recovers the true 0.70 slope cleanly (Target = 0.705, Noisy_target = 0.673), sharpening the 20×20 target resolution matrix toward the identity (Figure 5.4).
What if cues themselves vary trial-by-trial with x (stress_bold)? Under strong cue modulation (1.8 + 0.9 x), condition-mean subtraction (demix_ridge = 0.05) leaves residual cue variation (Cue_only = 0.488), whereas lowering demix_ridge = 0.02 activates joint 2nd-order Tikhonov (T, O) de-mixing—cutting Cue_only bleed to 0.074 (Target = 0.773) at the expected cost of ~45% larger trial SEs (0.101 vs. 0.070; Figure 5.2).







Figure 5.2: Estimated feedback slopes in the null-feedback Cue_only voxel under constant cue amplitude (left) versus trial-varying cue amplitude correlated with x (right), comparing default condition-mean de-mixing (0.05) against joint trial-level de-mixing (0.02).

5.6.3 3. Variable-Duration Epochs: Rate vs. Time-Integrated Activity
When neural activity is sustained at a constant firing rate (1.8 units/s) across variable decision durations (0.4–2.8 s), total evoked BOLD scales roughly linearly with duration. How Step 3 parameterizes source_model determines what scientific question is answered (Figure 5.5):

source_model = "impulse" misinterprets longer-duration BOLD accumulation as larger impulse height, creating a strong artificial positive slope against RT (beta = 1.392).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "rate" matches both the forward boxcar and midpoint readout window to each trial’s duration and uses a centered-subspace penalty plus Sherman–Morrison rank-1 baseline adjustment so constant firing rate remains invariant to RT (beta = 0.015, near true 0.00!).
source_model = "duration", duration_scale = "integral" normalizes each forward boxcar to unit area, explicitly estimating time-integrated neural mass (1.8 × duration, recovering slope 1.806 vs. true 1.800).







Figure 5.5: Same simulated constant-rate variable-duration BOLD series analyzed under three source specifications: impulse height (left), duration-matched rate (middle), and duration-integrated neural mass (right).





5.6.4 4. Optional Cross-Lag De-Mixing, Exact Analytical SEs, Precision Weights, and ZCA
Enabling demix_within_trial = TRUE applies a symmetric 2nd-order Tikhonov inverse across lags, sharpening single-subject lag specificity while increasing conditional lag SEs (Figure 5.6). Across all configurations, MEDuSA’s \(O(m_{\text{obs}} p M)\) AR operator factor compute_ar1_operator_factor() reproduces dense matrix covariance \(B \Sigma B^\top\) to 6.07e-18 and matches 2,500-draw Monte Carlo noise SDs trial by trial (Figure 5.7).
Finally, Step 3 combines per-trial measurement variance \(s_{ri}^2 = \text{se\_demixed}_{ri}^2\) with an Empirical-Bayes biological trial variance estimate \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) so precision_weight (\(w_{ri} \propto (\hat{\tau}_{\text{eff}}^2 + s_{ri}^2)^{-1}\)) downweights noisy edge/overlap trials smoothly without letting a single low-SE trial dominate when genuine biological trial variability is large (Figure 5.8), while regularized ZCA (whiten_panel = TRUE) suppresses off-diagonal within-run trial error correlations (Figure 5.9).






Figure 5.6: Effect of demix_within_trial = TRUE on estimated lag slopes (top) and conditional per-trial measurement SE (bottom).









Figure 5.7: Ratio of 2,500-draw Monte Carlo trial SD to analytical se_demixed across all 20 target trials in Run 1.









Figure 5.8: Pure measurement-only inverse-variance weights (precision_weight_op) versus biological-variance-stabilized Empirical-Bayes weights (precision_weight).









Figure 5.9: Within-run total trial correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after spectrum-continuous regularized ZCA (whiten_panel = TRUE).





Mathematical Reference: Composite Epoch Operator & Covariate Matching

For run \(r\), lag \(\tau\), valid observation rows \(I_r\), and frozen Step 2 inverse \(D_r \in \mathbb{R}^{n_r \times m_r}\):

Non-target subtraction: Let \(S_{r,0}\) read out all events at lag 0 and \(G_{r,0}\) be their column-centered forward HRF design. build_other_demix_operator() forms \(L_{\text{other}}\) (condition-mean least squares for demix_ridge >= 0.03, or 2nd-order iterated Tikhonov joint inversion for < 0.03), yielding cleaned target readout rows \(S_{\text{clean},\tau} = S_\tau - (S_\tau D_r G_{r,0,\text{other}}) L_{\text{other}}\).
Target cross-talk & duration baseline invariance: Given uncentered and column-centered target forward designs \((G_{\tau,\text{unc}}, G_\tau)\), solve_duration_demix_operator() row-normalizes \(R_{\text{unc}} = \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1} S_\tau D_r G_{\tau,\text{unc}}\), solves \((R_{\text{unc}}^\top R_{\text{unc}} + \lambda_{\text{demix}} Q_m + 10^{-8} I) W_{\text{unc}} = R_{\text{unc}}^\top \operatorname{diag}(g_{\text{safe}})^{-1}\) (penalizing only centered fluctuations \(Q_m = I_m - \frac{1}{m}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\)), applies a Sherman–Morrison rank-1 centering update to obtain \(W_\tau\), and restores centered diagonal gain \(\tilde{G}_\tau\).
Exact noise propagation & \(M_{\text{post}}\) alignment: The complete linear map from centered run BOLD to de-mixed target trials is \(B_{r,\tau} = \tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r\), with calibrated centered trial error covariance \(\Omega_{r,\tau} = \frac{\sigma_{\text{eff}}^2}{1 - 1/m} Q_m B_{r,\tau} C_{\text{obs}} \Sigma_{\text{AR}}[I_r, I_r] C_{\text{obs}}^\top B_{r,\tau}^\top Q_m\). Centered covariates \(X_{r,c}\) are multiplied by \(M_{\text{post}} = Q_m (\tilde{G}_\tau W_\tau S_{\text{clean},\tau} D_r G_\tau) Q_m\) prior to regression and ZCA whitening so predictor and response undergo identical off-diagonal target shrinkage.

title: Step 4: Parcel Aggregation and Analysis Panels
text:
6.1 Overview
Most cognitive neuroscience hypotheses are tested at the level of anatomical regions or functional parcels rather than noisy individual voxels. However, where and how you average across voxels matters enormously. Averaging raw BOLD before Step 1 blurs distinct intra-parcel vascular delays and cancels opposite-signed tuning only if signs oppose; conversely, fitting single-trial regressions voxel-by-voxel in Step 3 and averaging noisy beta estimates afterward throws away high-SNR parcel variance estimation (tau2_bio), distorts ZCA whitening, and ignores spatial noise correlations among neighboring voxels when computing parcel standard errors.
Step 4—executed seamlessly inside decon_epoch_regression(..., parcel_groups = parcel_ids)—aggregates continuous deconvolved activity across voxels within each parcel after voxel-specific deconvolution (preserving per-stratum HRFs and \(\text{AR}(p)\) whiteners) and before epoch de-mixing, Empirical-Bayes weighting, and ZCA whitening. Crucially, MEDuSA combines exact multi-stratum parcel operators (\(\sum_v u_v D_v F_v\)) with task-free whitened noise_innovations from Step 2 to measure true within-parcel spatial noise covariance—avoiding the classic pitfall where shared task-evoked activity inflates estimated parcel noise—and exports a tidy, self-contained panel carrying both within-unit (precision_weight) and cohort-comparable (precision_weight_cohort) weights plus cross-parcel shared_noise_loading vectors for Step 5–6 inference.

6.2 Goals of Step 4
Step 4 achieves four specific goals when transitioning from voxels to regional analysis panels:

Pool voxels using cross-run SNR-optimal weights (parcel_weights): Weight each parcel’s constituent voxels inversely by their cross-run observation-noise variance and upweight voxels with stronger cross-fitted Step 1 task \(R^2\), renormalizing automatically if a voxel drops out in one run.
Propagate true spatial noise correlation without task contamination: Compute each parcel’s effective observation-noise SD from Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations (\|Z_r (u \odot \sigma)\|_2), accurately spanning negative, independent, partially shared, and common spatial noise regimes.
Preserve mixed intra-parcel HRF strata exactly: Accumulate per-stratum forward/inverse operator contributions weighted by \(u_v\) whenever voxels inside a parcel belong to different (HRF, AR) strata, avoiding single-HRF approximation error.
Package a lossless, identity-safe trial panel for Steps 5–6: Deliver aligned raw, de-mixed, Empirical-Bayes-shrunk, and ZCA-whitened parcel columns alongside cohort-comparable precision weights and cross-parcel shared-error loadings.

What Step 4 deliberately leaves to Steps 5–6: Step 4 produces one participant’s parcel panel (and operator summaries). You must attach an explicit participant id column (and session if longitudinal) before stacking participants with data.table::rbindlist() for Step 5–6 population models.

Per-parcel loading vector reproducing cross-parcel noise correlations (\(R_{\text{err}} \approx \ell \ell^\top\))
data.table::rbindlist() drops matrix attributes attached to individual subject panels. Embedding shared_noise_loading as a column ensures cross-parcel noise covariance survives stacking (and full RDS/parquet/CSV workflows) for Step 6 shared_error = "auto"!

text:
6.6 Step 4 Mechanisms Illustrated

6.6.1 1. Precision- & Evidence-Weighted Voxel Aggregation (and Missing-Voxel Renormalization)
Within each parcel \(g\), Step 4 computes fixed cross-run nominal voxel weights \(u_v \propto \frac{1 + \overline{R}^2_{\text{cv},v} / (0.05 + \text{med}(\overline{R}^2_{\text{cv}}))}{\max(\overline{\sigma}_v^2, 0.10\,\text{med}(\overline{\sigma}^2))}\) normalized to \(\sum_{v \in g} u_v = 1\). Quieter, task-responsive voxels contribute more than noisy edge voxels.
What happens if a voxel becomes invalid in one run (e.g., partial FoV dropout or coil artifact in Run 2)? MEDuSA renormalizes the remaining valid voxels in that run to sum to 1 (Figure 6.1). Because renormalization slightly shifts the spatial composition of a small parcel, always inspect decon$scaling[[r]]$status when voxel dropout is non-trivial.






Figure 6.1: Nominal four-voxel parcel weights in Run 1 (sd = 0.013, 0.018, 0.022, 0.032) and automatic renormalization in Run 2 when Voxel 1 is marked invalid.





6.6.2 2. Why Task-Free noise_innovations Are Essential for Parcel Standard Errors
Suppose four voxels in a parcel have weights \(u\) and marginal noise SDs \(\sigma\). If voxel errors were spatially independent, the parcel noise SD would be \(\sigma_{\text{ind}} = \sqrt{\sum_v u_v^2 \sigma_v^2}\) (0.0091 in simulate_step4.R); if all four voxels shared identical noise (\(\rho_{\text{spatial}} = 1\)), the parcel noise SD would nearly double to \(\sigma_{\text{ceil}} = \sum_v u_v \sigma_v\) (0.0171)!
If you tried to estimate spatial noise correlation from second differences of deconvolved activity (\(\Delta^2 \hat{a}\)), shared task-evoked neural activity across the parcel looks just like shared noise, pegging the estimate near the 0.0171 ceiling even when true noise is independent (0.000) or negatively correlated (-0.20)! By instead projecting u * sigma onto Step 2’s task-free whitened noise_innovations (\(\hat{\sigma}_{\text{parcel}} = \|Z_r (u \odot \sigma)\|_2\)), MEDuSA tracks the true spatial noise SD across all four regimes—including sub-independence negative correlation—to within a few ten-thousandths (Figure 6.2, Table 6.1), and reproduces analytical se_demixed to machine precision (9.71e-17).

6.6.3 3. Exact Multi-Stratum Parcel Operators When Intra-Parcel HRFs Differ
When Step 1 uses voxel-level HRF selection (pooling = "voxel") or separate noise_groups inside a parcel, two voxels in the same parcel can belong to different (HRF, AR) strata (for example, \(4\text{ s}\) and \(8\text{ s}\) peak delays). Approximating the parcel operator with a single averaged HRF \(\bar{h} = \frac{1}{2}(h_4 + h_8)\) produces a 16.6% waveform discrepancy because matrix inversion is nonlinear: \(\frac{1}{2}(D_1 F_1 + D_2 F_2) \neq D(\bar{h}) F(\bar{h})\)! Step 4 avoids this approximation by accumulating exact stratum-by-stratum forward/inverse products \(\sum_s w_s D_s F_s\) (Figure 6.3).






Figure 6.3: Exact multi-stratum parcel reconstruction (MEDuSA multi-stratum parcel operator) vs. a single averaged-HRF approximation when a two-voxel parcel mixes 4 s and 8 s HRFs.





6.6.4 4. Working Trial Variance (tau2_mode), Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage, and Paired ZCA
On the aggregated parcel series, Step 4 estimates latent trial-to-trial biological variance \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) ("marginal" from run-centered variance, lag-1 trial differences, and MAD minus expected operator noise; "residual" from covariate regression residuals minus \(\operatorname{tr}((I - P_X)\Omega)\)). Different \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{bio}}^2\) estimates adjust how steeply precision_weight varies across trials (Figure 6.4), govern decon_eb shrinkage toward the run mean (Figure 6.5), and set the biological covariance component \(\hat{\tau}_{\text{ZCA}}^2 M_{\text{post}} M_{\text{post}}^\top\) inside paired within-run ZCA whitening (Figure 6.6).






Figure 6.4: Relative precision_weight vs. se_demixed under "marginal" and "residual" working trial-variance modes.

Figure 6.6: Within-run parcel correlation matrix \(\Sigma_{\text{tot}}\) before and after paired regularized ZCA (Nearly common parcel, Run 1).





Mathematical Reference: Innovation Spatial Covariance & Cross-Parcel Loadings


Within-parcel effective noise variance: Let \(Z_r \in \mathbb{R}^{m_r \times V}\) denote Step 2’s column-unit-norm task-projected whitened innovations (colSums(Z_r^2) == 1). For parcel \(g\) with valid voxels \(V_g\), normalized weights \(u_g\), and voxel observation-noise SDs \(\sigma_{r,V_g}\), define \(\zeta_{r,g} = Z_{r,V_g} (u_g \odot \sigma_{r,V_g})\). Because \(\mathbb{E}[Z_{r,i}^\top Z_{r,j}] = R_{\text{spatial},ij}\), \(\|\zeta_{r,g}\|_2^2 = \sum_{i,j \in V_g} u_i u_j \sigma_i \sigma_j \hat{R}_{\text{spatial},ij}\) is an unbiased, task-free estimator of parcel observation-noise variance, bounded safely into \([0.05\,\sigma_{\text{ind}}^2, \sigma_{\text{ceil}}^2]\).
Cross-parcel shared_noise_loading: Normalizing \(\tilde{z}_{r,g} = \zeta_{r,g} / \|\zeta_{r,g}\|_2\) and pooling \(\tilde{Z}_r^\top \tilde{Z}_r\) across runs (weighted by residual degrees of freedom, adjusted for inter-stratum operator overlap, Empirical-Bayes shrunk toward zero on noisy off-diagonals, and projected onto the PSD cone) yields unit_error_cor, whose principal factor loadings are stored in panel$shared_noise_loading for Step 6.

title: Step 5 · Group and trajectory inference
text:
Overview
Step 4 produces a participant-level trial panel in which each parcel, trial, and peri-event lag carries a deconvolved neural readout alongside propagated measurement-error and precision metadata. Step 5 tests whether trial-level behavioral associations generalize across the participant population—and characterizes how those effects unfold over peri-event time.
MEDuSA provides two complementary group-inference pathways in Step 5, matched to two distinct scientific targets:

title: Step 5 · Group and trajectory inference
text:
Split-wise linear mixed-effects models via mixed_by(): Fits a prespecified multilevel regression formula independently at each (parcel, evt_time) readout. This pathway is designed for rich within-trial factorial designs, cross-level interactions, random participant slopes, nested run intercepts, and precision-weighted single-readout inference, followed by explicit multiplicity correction across the planned (parcel, lag, term) family.
Joint multi-lag trajectory inference via medusa_multilag_infer(): Models all peri-event lags of a (parcel, term) profile jointly, combining participant-level within-run multiple regressions with available-case cross-lag covariance pooling, optional spectral resolution deblurring and P-spline smoothing, studentized Wishart null calibration (Max-|T|, 1D TFCE, omnibus Mahalanobis), simultaneous confidence bands, planned time-window contrasts, and peak/latency summaries.




Scientific question
Recommended Step 5 pathway
Primary inferential output

coef_df_reml + explicit familywise ("holm") or arbitrary-dependence FDR ("BY") adjustment


Which individual peri-event lags show an effect while controlling familywise error across the epoch?

Is there a temporally extended, same-sign deflection across neighboring lags?

Is there any evidence against a flat zero trajectory across the entire epoch?

title: Step 5 · Group and trajectory inference
text:
Goals of Step 5
Step 5 is designed to accomplish five methodological goals:

Separate within-person state fluctuations from between-person trait differences: Decompose trial predictors into within-participant (or within-run) deviations and participant means so cross-sectional baseline differences cannot confound or reverse phasic trial slopes.
Treat participants—not trials—as the unit of population replication: Account for inter-individual slope heterogeneity via participant random slopes in mixed_by() or precision-weighted random-effects slope pooling in medusa_multilag_infer(), preventing the severe Type I error inflation of naive trial-row regressions.
Propagate trial- and cohort-level reliability without discarding biological variance: Weight observations using total inverse variance \((\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) (precision_weight_cohort) rather than raw measurement inverse variance \(1/s_i^2\), and preserve exact linear design correspondence when analyzing ZCA-whitened panels (*_whitened).
Exploit cross-lag covariance for trajectory estimation and inference: Use the Step 3/4 lag resolution (\(R_{\mathrm{lag}}\)) and lag error correlation (\(C_{\mathrm{lag}}\)) operators alongside empirical cross-lag slope covariance to construct calibrated simultaneous bands, 1D TFCE statistics, omnibus epoch tests, and covariance-aware window contrasts.
Enforce transparent multiplicity control: Distinguish clearly between pointwise uncertainty at a single prespecified readout, trajectory-level familywise error across lags of one (parcel, term) curve, and study-wide multiplicity across multiple parcels, covariates, and contrasts.

What Step 5 leaves outside scope: Step 5 treats neural activity as the dependent outcome predicted by behavioral or experimental variables treated as known without measurement error. When deconvolved neural activity is moved to the right-hand side to predict another brain region (Target ~ Seed * Task) or behavioral response, ordinary mixed models and medusa_multilag_infer() do not correct predictor attenuation bias or shared seed–target measurement noise; those questions belong to Step 6. In addition, Step 5 conditions on the HRF, inverse, and parcel operators learned in Steps 1–4.

Inputs: What Step 5 Receives and Why
Step 5 accepts three structured input representations depending on which modeling pathway you choose and how upstream participant results were stored:



Input
Structure
Why Step 5 needs it and why it is shaped that way




subject_epochs (recommended for medusa_multilag_infer())
Named list of per-participant decon_epoch_regression() S3 objects
Preserves both each participant’s $panel and their exact parcel-level $lag_resolution, $lag_error_cor, and $demix_within_trial metadata. Passing the full list avoids losing operator matrices when panels are stacked or saved to CSV, and allows medusa_multilag_infer() to pool participant-specific lag operators automatically.


group_panel (required for mixed_by(), also accepted by medusa_multilag_infer())
Stacked long data.table keyed uniquely by (id, run, event_index, evt_time, parcel)
Gives mixed_by() a single rectangular table that can be split cleanly by (parcel, evt_time) while retaining behavioral covariates, run identifiers, precision_weight_cohort, and paired *_whitened columns. Keying behavioral merges on (id, run, event_index)—never trial alone—guarantees exact alignment when trials are dropped or runs are numbered per person.


subject_slopes (optional route for medusa_multilag_infer())
Long data.frame / data.table with (id, parcel, term, lag, estimate, std.error, df)
Allows users who fit custom within-participant first-stage models (e.g., generalized linear models, nonlinear computational fits, or custom nuisance designs) to bring per-participant lag slopes and SEs into medusa_multilag_infer() alongside explicit lag_resolution and lag_error_cor matrices.


Centered behavioral predictors
Within-person / within-run deviations (x_within) + person means (x_mean)
Computed on the behavioral trial table before merging with parcel activity so censored or missing fMRI frames in one parcel cannot shift the definition of a participant’s behavioral mean in another parcel.


contrasts & tr
Named list of early/late lag windows + acquisition TR (seconds)
Defines planned scientific window comparisons before inspecting trajectories and supplies reference operator timing if standalone tables lack operator attributes.



Before fitting any group model, verify that (id, run, event_index) is unique in the behavioral table and (id, run, event_index, evt_time, parcel) is unique in the merged panel:


Show trial-key verification and behavioral centering
key <- c("id", "run", "event_index")
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(trial_behavior[, ..key]))

trial_behavior[, `:=`(
  value_mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  value_within = value - mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
  entropy_within = entropy - mean(entropy, na.rm = TRUE)
), by = id]

group_panel <- merge(
  activity_panel,
  trial_behavior[, .(id, run, event_index, value_mean, value_within, entropy_within)],
  by = key, all.x = TRUE
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(group_panel[, .(id, run, event_index, evt_time, parcel)]))
