text:
Recommended Settings

Pathway A: Split-wise mixed models (mixed_by())

library(medusa)

group_formula <- decon_demixed ~ value_within + value_mean + entropy_within +
  (1 + value_within + entropy_within || id) + (1 | id:run)

group_models <- mixed_by(
  group_panel,
  model_formulae = list(trial_effects = group_formula),
  split_on = c("parcel", "evt_time"),
  weights = "precision_weight_cohort",
  calculate = "parameter_estimates_reml",
  padjust_by = NULL,
  tidy_args = list(effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE),
  return_models = TRUE
)

# Apply multiplicity correction across the exact planned family of focal terms
focal_tests <- subset(
  group_models$coef_df_reml,
  term %in% c("value_within", "entropy_within")
)
focal_tests$p_by <- p.adjust(focal_tests$p.value, method = "BY")



Pathway B: Joint multi-lag trajectory inference (medusa_multilag_infer())

# Upstream in Step 3/4: set demix_within_trial = FALSE when feeding medusa_multilag_infer()
# so cross-lag resolution R_lag is handled once at the group trajectory stage.
trajectory <- medusa_multilag_infer(
  subject_epochs,
  covariates = c("value_within", "entropy_within"),
  trajectory_mode = "auto",
  contrast_source = "unsmoothed",
  use_whitened = FALSE,
  tr = acquisition_tr,
  contrasts = list(late_minus_early = list(early = c(0, 1), late = c(3, 4))),
  n_perm = 4000L,
  n_boot_latency = 400L,
  seed = 6205L
)




Parameter / Choice
Package default
Recommended setting
Why and when to adjust




weights (in mixed_by())
NULL
"precision_weight_cohort"
Normalizes \((\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) once across the entire (parcel, evt_time) split rather than per person, preserving both within-run trial heteroskedasticity and between-participant SNR differences. Use "precision_weight" only if you intentionally want every participant weighted equally regardless of scan noise. Never pass 1 / se_demixed^2 directly (ignores biological trial variance).


Random-effects grouping
User formula
(1 + x_within || id) + (1 | id:run)
Includes random participant slopes for within-person focal predictors (preventing trial-row pseudoreplication) and nested participant–run intercepts (1 | id:run). Never write (1 | run) when run labels like "run1" repeat across participants.


Upstream demix_within_trial
TRUE (in Step 3)
TRUE for mixed_by(); FALSE for medusa_multilag_infer()
mixed_by() visits one lag at a time and relies on Step 3’s ridge demixing; medusa_multilag_infer() sees the entire lag profile and performs regularized spectral deblurring (trajectory_mode = "auto") with full cross-lag covariance propagation, avoiding double-regularization.


covariates (in medusa_multilag_infer())
Required
Pass correlated trial predictors jointly (c("value_within", "entropy_within"))
Time-varying covariates supplied together are fit jointly in a single within-run multiple regression (controlling shared variance), while participant-constant covariates (e.g., value_mean, age) are automatically routed to Level-2 precision-weighted WLS with HC2 SEs.


trajectory_mode
"auto"
"auto"
Automatically applies regularized spectral deblurring when demix_within_trial = FALSE (skipping deblurring if already demixed upstream) followed by cross-lag covariance-aware P-spline smoothing. Use "none" when evaluating raw lag readouts without spectral or spline post-processing.


contrast_source
"unsmoothed"
"unsmoothed"
Evaluates planned window contrasts on the deblurred trajectory prior to P-spline smoothing, retaining resolution recovery without introducing smoothing shrinkage bias into linear window averages.


use_whitened
FALSE
FALSE (or TRUE with all covariates pre-whitened in Step 4)
Unwhitened decon_demixed works out of the box with arbitrary formulas; if serial residual autocorrelation is strong in rapid designs, set whiten_panel = TRUE in Step 4 (passing all covariates so *_whitened columns exist) and match decon_demixed_whitened to *_whitened predictors.


Study-wide multiplicity
Within-term (mixed_by) / within-trajectory (multilag)
Explicit "BY" or "holm" across planned family
Built-in p_maxT and p_tfce control familywise error across lags within one (parcel, term) trajectory. When testing multiple parcels or terms, apply Holm or Benjamini–Yekutieli across the planned epoch omnibus_p values or across the planned (parcel, lag, term) table.

title: Step 5 · Group and trajectory inference
text:
Core Mechanisms in Detail

1. Separating within-person state slopes from between-person trait slopes
A raw trial-level predictor \(x_{sri}\) (participant \(s\), run \(r\), trial \(i\)) mixes phasic trial-to-trial variation around a person’s average with cross-sectional differences across people: \(x_{sri} = (x_{sri} - \bar x_s) + \bar x_s\). Comparing high- vs. low-value trials within the same person answers a fundamentally different biological question from comparing people who experience higher average value overall—and the two slopes can even have opposite signs.






Figure 7.1: Simulated participant means slope down across people even though the within-participant lines generally slope up. Only six within-participant series are shown for legibility.



In Figure 7.1, the true within-person trial slope is \(+0.55\) while the between-person trait slope is \(-0.72\). Fitting a single uncentered predictor estimates a confounded pooled slope of -0.432, whereas entering x_within and x_mean separately recovers 0.521 within participants and -0.731 between participants.






ImportantInterpreting between-person effects in MEDuSA



Keep two upstream conventions in mind whenever interpreting participant intercepts or trait covariates: 1. Run centering removes tonic run baselines: Step 2 scaling ("noise_sd", "demean", "zscore") centers BOLD within each run, so tonic run-constant neural baselines are not identifiable; between-person predictors (x_mean) explain differences in average event-locked phasic deflections across people, or cross-level interactions (x_within * trait) modulating within-person slopes. 2. HRF normalization conventions: Step 1 normalizes candidate HRFs to unit positive-lobe integral (normalize = "area"), so restored BOLD-unit amplitudes reflect the product of phasic neural amplitude and local neurovascular gain.


When a predictor drifts across runs (e.g., fatigue or block-level contingencies), centering within each (id, run) isolates pure within-run trial contrasts, while run-mean and person-mean terms can capture run- and person-level shifts separately.


2. Why participants—not trials—are the unit of population inference
For a single decomposed predictor, the canonical split-wise mixed model at one (parcel, evt_time) readout is:
\[
Y_{sri} = \beta_0 + \beta_W x^W_{sri} + \beta_B \bar x_s + b_{0s} + b_{Ws} x^W_{sri} + a_{sr} + \varepsilon_{sri}.
\]
Here \(b_{0s}\) captures persistent participant baseline deflection, \(a_{sr}\) captures participant-specific run shifts ((1 | id:run)), and \(b_{Ws}\) captures inter-individual heterogeneity in the within-person slope ((1 + x_within || id)). In a balanced design with \(S\) participants, \(m\) independent trials per participant, unit-variance centered predictor, slope heterogeneity \(\sigma_b^2\), and trial residual variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), the variance of the population slope estimate is:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_W) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{S} + \frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{Sm}.
\]
Collecting more trials \(m\) shrinks the second term toward zero, sharpening each person’s slope estimate, but leaves \(\sigma_b^2 / S\) untouched. Omitting random participant slopes—or running trial-row OLS—treats \(Sm\) trials as independent draws of the population slope and mistakes stable individual differences \(\sigma_b^2\) for population certainty.






Figure 7.2: Two tests of the same zero population slope in 3,000 simulations per trial count. The participant-slope test uses one slope per person. Trial-row OLS ignores within-person slope dependence. Bars show approximate 95% Monte Carlo error intervals.



In Figure 7.2 (12 participants, true population mean slope \(\beta_W = 0\), nonzero \(\sigma_b^2\)), naive trial-row OLS false-positive rates escalate with trial count—reaching 79.8% at 192 trials per person—whereas testing participant slopes holds nominal Type I error at 5.2%.


3. Propagating trial precision and matched trial-space whitening
Conditional on participant and run random effects, the observed trial response combines true biological trial-to-trial variability \(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{latent}}_{sr}\) and propagated Step 1–4 BOLD measurement error:
\[
R_{sr} = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{latent}}_{sr}) + \Omega_{sr}.
\]
In lme4::lmer(), prior weights \(w_i\) scale the conditional residual variance as \(\sigma^2 / w_i\). Step 4’s precision_weight_cohort sets \(w_i \propto (\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{eff}}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) across all runs and participants, and mixed_by() normalizes finite positive weights once over the complete-case split to mean 1.






Figure 7.3: For the same readout, the weighted model allows larger conditional residual spread in the noisier run. The unweighted fit imposes the same spread across both runs. The generating SD combines latent trial variation and measurement noise.



As Figure 7.3 shows, when Run 2 has higher measurement noise than Run 1 (true combined conditional SDs \(0.194\) and \(0.403\)), precision-weighted lmer() recovers conditional residual scales matching both runs (\(0.191\) and \(0.396\)), downweighting noisy trials and noisy scans appropriately instead of forcing a single pooled residual SD (\(0.313\)).


Matched linear transformations when using ZCA-whitened panels (*_whitened)

When trial-to-trial measurement errors remain serially correlated across closely spaced events, Step 4’s whiten_panel = TRUE applies a run-mean-preserving regularized ZCA map \(T = P + \Phi Q\) (where \(P\) projects onto the run mean and \(Q = I - P\) centers within run) identically to the response (decon_demixed_whitened) and to every covariate supplied to Step 4 (*_whitened). Because \(T \mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\), run intercepts remain intact, while both fixed and random slopes for within-run predictors operate on the exact transformed design columns \(T x\).
Two rules are essential whenever use_whitened = TRUE or decon_demixed_whitened is modeled: 1. Never mix coordinates: Always pair decon_demixed_whitened with *_whitened predictors from the same (parcel, evt_time) split; regressing whitened activity on unwhitened time-varying covariates estimates a mismatched slope. 2. Form interactions before whitening: Because \(T(x \odot z) \neq (Tx) \odot (Tz)\), construct any within-run product or polynomial columns before calling decon_epoch_regression(..., whiten_panel = TRUE) so Step 4 transforms the interaction column directly.

Always audit fitted models across splits—checking participant support, lme4::isSingular() flags, and within-run conditional lag-1 residual correlations (Figure 7.4):


Show split-level model audit code
fits <- lapply(group_models$models$model, function(entry) entry$reml)
group_models$models[, .(
  parcel, evt_time,
  trials = vapply(fits, nobs, numeric(1)),
  participants = vapply(fits, function(fit) nlevels(model.frame(fit)$id), integer(1)),
  singular = vapply(fits, lme4::isSingular, logical(1))
)]








Figure 7.4: Lag-one correlations of scaled conditional residuals in the focal model, computed separately for each participant and run. Even with independent generating residuals at this readout, 24 trials per run produce noisy correlation estimates.





4. Split-wise profiles and defining the multiplicity family
Fitting mixed_by() across 3 simulated parcels (Phasic, Sustained, Null) and 8 peri-event lags (\(-2\text{ s}\) to \(+5\text{ s}\)) for 24 participants yields 24 REML fits (0 singular) and \(3 \times 8 \times 2 = 48\) planned focal tests across value_within and entropy_within.






Figure 7.5: Three simulated parcel profiles. Dashed lines show known population slopes, and ribbons are pointwise 95% Satterthwaite t intervals. All panels share a vertical scale.









Figure 7.6: The same 48 tests arranged as parcel-by-lag cells. Teal cells pass BY across the entire family. Orange cells meet the unadjusted 0.05 cutoff only.



In Figure 7.5 and Figure 7.6, 9 cells pass the unadjusted \(p \le .05\) threshold—including isolated false positives on zero-truth lags—whereas 7 cells survive Benjamini–Yekutieli ("BY") FDR control across the full 48-test family, cleanly isolating the phasic value_within peak around \(+1\text{ s}\) and the sustained entropy_within plateau across \(+1\text{ to }+4\text{ s}\). Because adjacent lags are positively correlated, "BY" guarantees FDR control under arbitrary dependence, though its harmonic-sum penalty makes it conservative when lag grids are dense—motivating the joint trajectory estimator below.

title: Step 5 · Group and trajectory inference
text:
Joint Trajectory Inference (medusa_multilag_infer())
Rather than treating the 8 lags of a parcel profile as unrelated split-wise regressions, medusa_multilag_infer() estimates and tests the entire lag vector \(\widehat b = (\widehat b_1, \dots, \widehat b_L)^\top\) jointly using its cross-lag covariance \(\Sigma_b\).

1. Within-subject joint regression, available-case pooling, and spectral deblurring

Joint within-run multiple regression & Level-2 trait routing: When given subject_epochs or group_panel, medusa_multilag_infer() fits all supplied time-varying covariates jointly in a precision-weighted within-run multiple regression at each lag (applying matched \(M_{\text{post}}\) predictor projection if Step 3 target demixing was active), blending model-based and heteroskedasticity-robust slope SEs. Any between-participant constant predictors are automatically fit at Level 2 via precision-weighted WLS with HC2 leverage-adjusted SEs.
Available-case cross-lag pooling: Participants who miss edge lags (for instance, due to run-boundary clipping or Step 3’s obs_frac_tau < 0.20 censoring gate) are retained at all supported interior lags rather than dropped listwise. At each lag \(\ell\), participant slopes \(b_{s\ell}\) are pooled with random-effects precision weights \((\widehat\tau_\ell^2 + s_{s\ell}^2)^{-1}\), and pairwise cross-lag correlations shrink empirical slope correlations toward the working operator correlation before eigenvalue flooring.
Spectral resolution deblurring and P-spline smoothing: Under trajectory_mode = "auto", when upstream demix_within_trial = FALSE, medusa_multilag_infer() applies a regularized spectral inverse of the Step 3/4 cross-lag resolution matrix \(R_{\mathrm{lag}}\) ("deblur", normalized to preserve local lobe gain) followed by covariance-aware boosted P-spline smoothing ("deblur_pspline"). Its processed trajectory covariance \(\Sigma_{\mathrm{multilag}}\) incorporates a Marra–Wood posterior smoothing-bias variance component rather than naive plug-in sandwich shrinkage.







Figure 7.7: Deterministic coefficient-table example. The supplied resolution matrix spreads the known phasic target across adjacent lags. The deblurred curve nearly overlaps the known target in this example. Recovery depends on regularization and on the matrix representing the actual readout.





Show the custom subject coefficient-table route
partial_trajectory <- medusa_multilag_infer(
  subject_slopes,
  lag_resolution = resolution_by_parcel,
  lag_error_cor = error_cor_by_parcel,
  trajectory_mode = "deblur",
  n_perm = 4000L,
  n_boot_latency = 0L,
  seed = 6205L
)




2. Studentized Wishart calibration: Max-|T|, 1D TFCE, and Omnibus tests
To account for finite-sample uncertainty in the estimated \(L \times L\) cross-lag covariance across participants, medusa_multilag_infer() calibrates trajectory statistics using n_perm studentized Wishart covariance draws (with plus-one Monte Carlo \(p\)-values):

Max-|T| and simultaneous bands (p_maxT, conf.low.sim, conf.high.sim): Compares each lag’s absolute studentized statistic against the distribution of \(\max_\ell |T_\ell|\) across the epoch. The resulting simultaneous 95% band covers the entire true trajectory across all lags jointly with 95% probability, unlike narrower pointwise ribbons.
1D TFCE (p_tfce): Integrates statistic height and contiguous same-sign cluster extent across thresholds along the ordered lag grid, boosting sensitivity to sustained deflections (Sustained parcel) without arbitrary cluster-forming cutoffs. Because TFCE borrows support across neighboring lags, a small p_tfce establishes presence of an extended cluster rather than exact lag onset.
Epoch Omnibus (omnibus_p): Evaluates a regularized Mahalanobis quadratic form across the full raw lag vector to test whether the epoch departs from zero anywhere.







Figure 7.8: Raw lag estimates, pointwise intervals, and the raw simultaneous Max-|T| band from the panel route. The orange curve is the P-spline used for shape and the planned window contrast. The known synthetic panel has no deconvolution blur, so this example uses P-spline smoothing alone.









Figure 7.9: The smallest within-trajectory Max-|T| and TFCE p-values and the epoch omnibus p-value for three simulated parcel–term pairs. The vertical reference is 0.05. Values at the Monte Carlo floor use 4,000 draws.



In the live demonstration (Figure 7.8 and Figure 7.9), both true signals—Phasic value_within and Sustained entropy_within—hit the 4,000-draw Monte Carlo floor (min_p_maxT = 0.0002, min_p_tfce = 0.0002, omnibus_p = 0.0005), while every null parcel–term trajectory remains well above .05 (Null entropy_within: omnibus_p = 0.269, min_p_maxT = 0.423, min_p_tfce = 0.438). See the Multi-lag trajectory calibration chapter for 180-replicate empirical Type I error and simultaneous-band coverage results across complete and gapped/serially correlated panels.


3. Planned window contrasts and continuous timing summaries
When a hypothesis compares early vs. late epoch phases (contrasts = list(late_minus_early = list(early = c(0, 1), late = c(3, 4)))), medusa_multilag_infer() evaluates \(c^\top \widehat b_*\) with SE \(\sqrt{c^\top \Sigma_* c}\) on the curve selected by contrast_source:



contrast_source
Trajectory evaluated
When to use




"unsmoothed" (recommended default)
After spectral deblurring (if active), before P-spline smoothing
Preserves resolution deblurring gains without letting P-spline curvature shrinkage pull early and late window means toward each other.


"raw"
Original group lag estimates before cross-lag operators
Purest test of raw lag averages when no spectral deblurring is desired.


"multilag"
Final processed curve after deblurring + P-spline smoothing
Descriptive contrast of the plotted smooth curve itself (see worked contrast comparison).



In our simulated panel, the late_minus_early ([3, 4] s minus [0, 1] s) contrast cleanly separates the decaying phasic value response (estimate = -0.177, \(t_{23} = -7.49\), \(p = 1.3e-07\)) from the rising sustained entropy response (estimate = 0.082, \(t_{23} = 4.26\), \(p = 0.0003\)).
Finally, $latency interpolates the processed trajectory on a natural cubic spline (fine_dt = 0.01 s) to estimate continuous peak_lag, squared-amplitude center of mass (com_lag), and contiguous half-height width (fwhm), propagating uncertainty via n_boot_latency parametric draws from the trajectory covariance. For Phasic value_within, the grid maximum sits at 1.00 s and the spline peak at 1.02 s (95% CI [0.92, 1.11] s, FWHM 2.10 s), whereas Sustained entropy_within exhibits a broader center of mass at 2.45 s and FWHM 3.94 s. Always treat sub-TR decimal timing as smooth curve interpolation bounded by upstream HRF and inverse resolution, and require a well-defined signal (omnibus_p / p_maxT) before interpreting peak latency; on flat null curves, peak location spans the entire epoch window.

title: Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI
text:
Overview
In Step 5, deconvolved neural activity sits on the left-hand side of the regression (Neural ~ Behavior), where zero-mean BOLD measurement noise inflates standard errors without biasing population slope estimates. Step 6 moves a deconvolved parcel readout onto the right-hand side (Target ~ Seed + Task + Seed:Task) to test trial-to-trial functional connectivity and psychophysiological interaction (PPI)—or brain-to-behavior prediction (Behavior ~ Seed).
Placing a noisy deconvolved estimate on the right-hand side creates two immediate statistical hazards that ordinary OLS and lmer() cannot fix:
Step 6 (decon_connectivity_repair(), backed by medusa_fit_mmom()) addresses these hazards by pairing Step 4’s analytical per-trial error variances (se_demixed^2) and task-free cross-parcel noise innovation correlations (shared_noise_loading / unit_error_cor) with Method-of-Moments with Step-up Regularization (M-MOMS) inside each participant, followed by leverage-guarded Hartung–Knapp–Sidik–Jonkman (HKSJ) random-effects pooling across participants.
crumbs: 8  Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI

title: Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI
text:
Predictor attenuation bias: Trial-level measurement error \(u_i\) in the seed inflates the observed design variance \(X^\top X\), systematically shrinking both the baseline seed connectivity slope and the Seed:Task PPI slope toward zero.
Spurious coupling from shared cross-parcel noise: Scanner drift, physiological pulsatility, head motion, and overlapping vascular noise create correlated measurement errors \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i) \neq 0\) between seed and target parcels. Disattenuating the denominator without subtracting shared seed–target noise in the numerator amplifies false connectivity—and if shared error varies with task condition, it can manufacture a completely spurious PPI.
crumbs: 8  Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI

title: Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI
text:
Goals of Step 6
Step 6 is designed to accomplish four specific goals:

Disattenuate noisy neural predictors and PPI interactions: Construct exact per-trial \(q \times q\) predictor measurement-error covariance blocks \(\Psi_i\)—including the off-diagonal error covariance \(x_i s_i^2\) between a noisy seed \(\widehat S_i\) and its task product \(\widehat S_i x_i\)—and subtract them from observed design moments via medusa_fit_mmom().
Subtract stationary cross-parcel shared measurement error automatically: Use Step 4’s task-free unit_error_cor matrix or shared_noise_loading vectors (shared_error = "auto") to estimate per-trial seed–target error covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i)\) (err_xy) without stripping genuine task-evoked neural coupling.
Preserve clear direct vs. reduced-form PPI estimands: Let the analyst choose explicitly whether the seed retains its linear task response (orthogonalize_seed_x = FALSE, isolating direct connectivity and linear modulation) or is residualized against task covariates with exact error-covariance projection (orthogonalize_seed_x = TRUE).
Pool participant slopes with finite-sample random-effects calibration: Aggregate participant-level M-MOMS slopes at the group level using HKSJ / HC2 leverage-adjusted random-effects inference, treating independent participants as the unit of replication while guarding against extreme low-reliability outlier weights.

What Step 6 leaves outside scope (and requires you to check): Step 6 corrects within-trial additive second-moment measurement error conditional on the operators learned in Steps 1–4. It does not undo unequal cross-parcel source resolution biases (\(K_S \neq K_T\)), model full cross-trial off-diagonal error blocks simultaneously inside M-MOMS, or automatically detect condition-dependent changes in shared physiological/motion noise (\(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i)\) varying with \(x_i\)). Because task-modulated shared error is indistinguishable from latent PPI using marginal trial SEs alone, Step 6 pairs estimation with explicit shared-error sensitivity diagnostics. For deeper theoretical derivations and full-covariance research prototypes, see From BOLD noise to M-MOM error variances and Measurement-error models and REPAIR.

title: Step 6 · Trial-level connectivity and PPI
text:
Core Mechanisms in Detail

1. The structural trial model and M-MOMS moment correction
For participant \(s\) and trial \(i\) (after centering seed, target, and task covariates within each participant and run), let \(S_i\) be latent seed activity at seed_lag, \(T_i\) latent target activity at target_lag, and \(x_i\) an error-free centered task modulator:
\[
T_i = \beta_S S_i + \beta_x x_i + \beta_P (S_i x_i) + \varepsilon_i.
\]
Here \(\beta_S\) is baseline trial-to-trial coupling at \(x_i = 0\), and \(\beta_P\) is the psychophysiological interaction slope—how much the seed–target slope changes per unit change in \(x_i\) (for \(x_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), \(2\beta_P\) is the slope difference between conditions). Always include both main effects (\(\beta_S\) and \(\beta_x\)) when testing \(\beta_P\) so shared main-effect task activation is not absorbed into the interaction.
Because Step 4 observes noisy readouts \(W_i = S_i + u_i\) and \(Y_i = T_i + v_i\) rather than \((S_i, T_i)\), the observed regressor vector \(X_i = [W_i,\, x_i,\, W_i x_i]^\top\) carries measurement error \(e_{X,i} = [u_i,\, 0,\, x_i u_i]^\top\). Even when \(u_i\) is purely univariate on each trial with variance \(s_i^2 = \texttt{se\_demixed}_i^2\), the seed column and the PPI interaction column share the same noise realization \(u_i\), creating a structured \(3 \times 3\) predictor error covariance block on trial \(i\):
\[
\Psi_i = \operatorname{Cov}(e_{X,i} \mid x_i) = s_i^2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & x_i \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ x_i & 0 & x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Notice two essential features of \(\Psi_i\): - Heteroskedastic interaction error: Trial measurement variance in the PPI column scales with \(x_i^2 s_i^2\), so extreme modulator trials carry amplified measurement noise. - Signed predictor–interaction error covariance: Whenever \(x_i \neq 0\), the off-diagonal entry \(x_i s_i^2\) is nonzero (and negative when \(x_i < 0\)). Passing diagonal SEs without this off-diagonal term miscalibrates both main and interaction slopes.
Meanwhile, if seed and target measurement errors correlate (\(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = c_i\)), the observed cross-product \(X^\top Y\) is also biased by \(\sum_i [c_i,\, 0,\, x_i c_i]^\top\). M-MOMS solves the bias-corrected normal equations (with step-up eigenvalue regularization when \(X^\top X - \sum_i \Psi_i\) nears singularity):
\[
\left(X^\top X - \sum_{i=1}^n \Psi_i\right) \widehat\beta = X^\top Y - \sum_{i=1}^n \begin{pmatrix} \operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) \\ 0 \\ x_i \operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Under shared_error = "auto", decon_connectivity_repair() populates \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i) = \widehat r_{ST} \, s_{S,i} s_{T,i}\) using participant \(s\)’s task-free innovation correlation \(\widehat r_{ST}\) from Step 4 (unit_error_cor, or the inner product of shared_noise_loading vectors). That automatically removes stationary cross-parcel background noise correlation without needing resting-state scans or manual calibration.


2. Disattenuation vs. task-dependent shared error: two controlled stress tests
Why isn’t stationary shared_error = "auto"—or marginal SE disattenuation alone—an automatic guarantee for every PPI claim? Consider two panel-level simulations (120 datasets each; 16 participants, 2 runs, 60 trials/run, balanced \(x_i \in \{-1, +1\}\), marginal seed and target measurement error SDs fixed identically at \(0.70\) in every condition):

Genuine PPI (independent errors): True population interaction \(\beta_P = 0.35\), independent seed–target errors (\(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = 0\)).
Task-modulated shared-error null: True population interaction \(\beta_P = 0\), zero average error correlation across the run, but shared error flips sign with task condition: \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i \mid x_i) = 0.65 x_i \sigma^2\) (for example, condition-locked breath-hold, arousal, or head-jerking artifacts affecting both regions during \(x_i = +1\) trials). Because average unconditional \(\operatorname{Cov}(u, v) = 0\) across balanced \(-1/+1\) trials, neither marginal SEs (se_demixed) nor a single stationary run-wide correlation (shared_error = "auto") sees the condition-flipped cross-error!

The two panels of Figure 8.1 illustrate both sides of measurement-error correction:

When measurement error is genuinely disattenuated (Genuine PPI): Naive regression is severely attenuated (0.230 vs. truth 0.350, 0.0% CI coverage because narrow group SEs center on the biased value). 3. Sensitivity analysis and reporting checklist for Step 6
Because stationary background noise correlation (shared_error = "auto") removes baseline cross-parcel shared error \(\operatorname{Cov}(u, v) = r_0 \sigma_S \sigma_T\) (which biases main-effect seed connectivity) while condition-modulated cross-error \(\Delta r \cdot x_i \sigma_S \sigma_T\) threatens ppi, every empirical PPI claim should evaluate how sensitive its conclusion is to plausible condition-dependent error correlation:






Figure 8.2: Population moment sensitivity in the shared-error null. The hypothetical cross-error correlation changes sign with the task condition. At the generating amplitude of 0.65 the corrected slope crosses zero.



As Figure 8.2 shows, plotting the implied M-MOMS interaction slope across a range of hypothetical task-modulated cross-error correlations \(r(x)\) immediately reveals how strong condition-locked artifact coupling would have to be to explain away an observed PPI effect. Pair this sensitivity check with physiological/motion nuisance regressors in Step 1/2 (nuisance_list), framewise displacement stratified checks, and a negative-control reference parcel that shares vascular/physiological noise proximity without the hypothesized circuit connection.
When reporting a Step 6 connectivity or PPI analysis, always document:

Circuit & lag specification: Exact seed_region, target_region, seed_lag, target_lag, whether control_target_at_seed_lag was included, and the prespecified multiplicity family across region pairs and lags.
Covariate centering & orthogonalization: Coding of the modulator \(x_i\), included main effects, and whether orthogonalize_seed_x was FALSE (direct model) or TRUE (residualized-seed model).
Naive vs. M-MOMS comparison: Side-by-side naive_unweighted and mmoms estimates in identical coordinates (use_whitened = FALSE) so readers see both raw and disattenuated magnitudes.
Shared-error provenance & participant diagnostics: Summary of ppi$subjects$r_shared_error, shared_error_source, participant/trial counts, any mmoms step-up regularization triggers, and sensitivity to shared_error = "zero" vs. "auto" (plus condition-specific noise checks for PPI).

title: From BOLD noise to M-MOM error variances
text:
MEDuSA estimates how much observation noise enters each recovered trial activity estimate. When deconvolved neural activity becomes a predictor in Step 6 (Target ~ Seed * Task or Behavior ~ Neural), Method-of-Moments measurement-error correction (medusa_fit_mmom() / decon_connectivity_repair()) needs its measurement-error variance, typically se_demixed^2, expressed in the exact same units as the predictor. This trial-level measurement variance is distinct from the standard error of a fitted group regression coefficient.
\[
\underbrace{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\varepsilon)}_{\text{BOLD noise (Step 1)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\widehat\Omega_\tau}_{\text{trial error covariance (Steps 3–4)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{s_i=\sqrt{\widehat\Omega_{\tau,ii}}}_{\text{trial SE (`se_demixed`)}}
\ \longrightarrow\
\underbrace{\Psi_i}_{\text{M-MOM error block (Step 6)}}.
\]

1. Estimate the BOLD noise
For one run and voxel, write \(y = Hs + Z\gamma + \varepsilon\), with
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon) = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 \Sigma_{\rm cor}.
\]
Here \(H\) applies the selected HRF and \(Z\) contains nuisance terms. Step 1’s pooled AR(1) profile REML and shrunk residual AR(\(q\)) correction define a cascaded AR(\(p\)) temporal correlation model \(\Sigma_{\rm cor}\) (evaluated at the exact retained acquisition indices \(\Gamma_N[\text{rows}, \text{rows}]\) when frames are censored). The amplitude \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) is the marginal observation-noise SD, not the white-noise innovation SD.
In fit_crossrun_decon(), hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd() estimates \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) primarily from leverage-standardized, Winsorized GLS residuals after conditioning on the selected HRF and post-selection AR(\(p\)) correlation model (converting innovation scale to stationary marginal scale via hrf_ar_cascade_info()). As a standalone estimator for single-run deconvolve_reglin(), omitted-event safeguard, and low-degrees-of-freedom fallback, estimate_decon_noise_sd() estimates marginal noise amplitude from second differences \(d_t = y_t - 2y_{t-1} + y_{t-2}\), which suppress smooth BOLD signal:
\[
\widehat\sigma_{\rm obs}
=\frac{0.5\,\operatorname{SD}(d)+0.5\,\operatorname{MAD}_0(d)}
       {\sqrt{6-8\widehat r_1+2\widehat r_2}}.
\]
The normal-consistent MAD is centered at zero, and the denominator adjusts analytically for lag-1 and lag-2 autocorrelation. Crucially, BOLD noise is estimated prior to downstream behavioral or connectivity regressions.


2. Propagate noise through the linear inverse and epoch operators
With HRF, regularization penalty, frame weights, nuisance projection, and noise parameters held fixed, deconvolution is a linear map \(\widehat s = My\). Event interpolation, gain restoration, and Step 3’s cross-event and within-trial demixing combine with \(M\) into a linear trial-readout operator \(B_\tau\). Therefore, conditional on the learned operators,
\[
\Omega_{\tau,\rm raw}
=\sigma_{\rm eff}^2\,\widetilde B_\tau\Sigma_{\rm cor}\widetilde B_\tau^\top,
\]
where \(\widetilde B_\tau\) incorporates input run-centering and inverse nuisance/whitening projections. In our independent numerical verification (worked/mmom-check.R), MEDuSA’s operator-propagated cascade covariance matches an explicit stationary AR(3) Toeplitz reference to 1.11e-16.
Run-centered finite-sample calibration. Because downstream within-run regressions center trial series within each run, decon_epoch_regression() centers the propagated \(m \times m\) trial error covariance (\(m > 1\) valid trials) and applies a Bessel-like finite-sample calibration:
\[
Q_m = I_m - \frac{\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top}{m},\qquad
\widehat\Omega_\tau = \frac{Q_m\Omega_{\tau,\rm raw}Q_m}{1-1/m},
\] \[
\boxed{\texttt{se\_demixed}_i = \sqrt{\max(0, \widehat\Omega_{\tau,ii})}}.
\]
Thus se_demixed represents a run-centered, finite-sample-calibrated trial measurement SE. The full off-diagonal \(\widehat\Omega_\tau\) is used internally for biological variance estimation (tau2_bio) and optional ZCA panel whitening, while the panel exports diagonal se_demixed and adjacent-trial error autocorrelation error_ac1.

Keep units and spatial aggregation consistent
If \(d\) is the Step 2 scaling divisor, restore_scale = FALSE uses \(\sigma_{\rm eff} = \widehat\sigma_{\rm obs} / d\), whereas restore_scale = TRUE restores \(\sigma_{\rm eff} = \widehat\sigma_{\rm obs}\) so activity and se_demixed scale together. Rescaling a predictor by \(c\) requires rescaling its SE by \(|c|\) and its error variance by \(c^2\).
In Step 4, parcel aggregation forms precision-weighted parcel series using task-free Step 1 whitened noise_innovations to estimate both within-parcel spatial noise covariance (propagated through exact operator strata) and low-rank cross-parcel shared_noise_loading vectors that survive rbindlist() stacking.



3. Supply measurement-error moments to M-MOM
For an observed predictor \(\widehat a_i = a_i + u_i\), set \(\psi_i = \operatorname{Var}(u_i) = \texttt{se\_demixed}_i^2\). A single noisy neural predictor uses \(\Psi_i = [\psi_i]\). For a PPI design \((\widehat a_i,\, x_i,\, \widehat a_i x_i)\) with error-free modulator \(x_i\),
\[
\Psi_i = \psi_i
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & x_i\\
0 & 0 & 0\\
x_i & 0 & x_i^2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]



Exported quantity
Role in downstream modeling




se_demixed^2
Predictor measurement-error variance (\(\psi_i\)) for decon_demixed in M-MOM / M-MOMS


se_whitened^2
Transformed trial error variance for decon_demixed_whitened


shared_noise_loading / unit_error_cor
Task-free cross-parcel noise innovation basis used by shared_error = "auto" to estimate \(\operatorname{Cov}(u_i, v_i)\) (err_xy)


tau2_bio
Estimated latent biological trial-to-trial variance (not measurement error)


precision_weight / precision_weight_cohort
Inverse total trial variance \((\widehat\tau_{\rm eff}^2 + s_i^2)^{-1}\) for Step 5 outcome weighting (never substitute for \(\Psi_i\))


fit$coefficients$se
Standard error of an estimated M-MOM regression slope




Minimal applied interface (medusa_fit_mmom())
When decon_connectivity_repair() handles parcel-to-parcel connectivity and PPI automatically, it calls medusa_fit_mmom() under the hood. You can also call medusa_fit_mmom() directly when predicting a behavioral outcome (rt, choice log-odds score, pupillometry) from one or more deconvolved parcel readouts within a participant:

4. Distributional assumptions and scope conditions

Operator covariance propagation is distribution-free up to second moments: \(\operatorname{Cov}(B\varepsilon) = B\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)B^\top\) requires finite second moments and an accurate temporal/spatial noise correlation model, not Gaussianity—though Winsorized/MAD scale factors calibrate to Gaussian efficiency.
Single-subject M-MOM SEs are conditional model-based estimates: Within-subject SEs from repair::fit_mmom() / medusa_fit_mmom() use a normal-error variance formula conditional on first-stage error moments. Across multiple participants, decon_connectivity_repair() pools participant slopes via HKSJ random-effects inference so group \(p\)-values rely on between-participant replication rather than single-subject row independence.
Zero-mean measurement error vs. regularization bias: Propagating se_demixed^2 quantifies observation-noise variance \(B\Sigma_\varepsilon B^\top\), not source resolution bias \((R - I)s\) from ridge/difference regularization or HRF mismatch. When seed and target parcels experience substantially different temporal smoothing (\(R_S \neq R_T\)), disattenuating variance alone does not undo unequal resolution; see Measurement-error models and REPAIR for resolution-aware extensions.

title: Measurement-error models and REPAIR
text:
NoteHow this chapter relates to Step 6 in medusa



In medusa, decon_connectivity_repair(..., shared_error = "auto") implements per-trial M-MOMS predictor disattenuation, task-free cross-parcel shared_noise_loading / unit_error_cor error-moment subtraction (err_xy), and HKSJ participant-level random-effects pooling (Step 6). This research chapter investigates what lies beyond diagonal per-trial M-MOMS: unequal regional source resolution (\(K_s \neq K_t\)), full cross-trial error covariance blocks (\(\Omega_{ss}, \Omega_{st}\)), likelihood-only finite-basis source reconstruction, and participant-cluster estimating equations.



Summary of Findings
Attaching diagonal trial SEs to ordinary M-MOMS disattenuates independent white measurement noise, but full latent connectivity inference faces three deeper structural requirements: unbiased source resolution, cross-parcel/cross-trial shared-error moments, and participant-cluster uncertainty calibration.

Recover an unbiased source mean (or model resolution explicitly): Regularized continuous deconvolution yields \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat a_r \mid a_r] = K_r a_r\) with \(K_r \neq I\). In our controlled unequal-resolution experiment (\(K_s \neq K_t\)), full noise-moment subtraction alone estimated connectivity as 0.767 when truth was 0.550. Inverting known, well-conditioned resolution operators restored recovery to 0.551.
Propagate shared errors and cluster at the participant level: Under unbiased source measurements with strong serial (\(0.55\)) and shared cross-parcel (\(0.45\)) Gaussian noise, the full cross-trial corrected-score estimator recovered 0.546. Participant-cluster intervals covered truth in 94.8% of repetitions, whereas row-based intervals covered only 86.0%.
Respect finite-participant limits: With only 12 participants, asymptotic cluster sandwich intervals undercovered (91.8% connectivity coverage)—motivating the HKSJ \(t\)-distribution small-sample pooling used in medusa::decon_connectivity_repair().



1. Define the neural relationship and the measurement relationship
For participant \(g\) and trial \(i\), define a centered task variable \(z_{gi}\) and latent source amplitudes:
\[
a_{t,gi}=\alpha_g+\beta a_{s,gi}+\gamma z_{gi}
               +\delta z_{gi}a_{s,gi}+\eta_{gi}.
\]
\(\beta\) is the seed–target association at \(z=0\); \(\delta\) is its task modulation (PPI). A general linear measurement interface across all trials of participant \(g\) is:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}\widehat a_{s,g}\\\widehat a_{t,g}\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}K_{s,g}&0\\0&K_{t,g}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}a_{s,g}\\a_{t,g}\end{bmatrix}
+\begin{bmatrix}u_g\\v_g\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\!\begin{pmatrix}u_g\\v_g\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}\Omega_{ss,g}&\Omega_{st,g}\\
\Omega_{st,g}^{\top}&\Omega_{tt,g}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Classical additive measurement-error correction assumes \(K_s = K_t = I\). In addition, PPI products and trial smoothing do not commute:
\[
K\,\operatorname{diag}(z)a_s \ne \operatorname{diag}(z)K a_s.
\]
Multiplying a smoothed or ZCA-whitened seed by the task modulator \(z\) afterward does not match smoothing the latent interaction—which is why decon_connectivity_repair() defaults to use_whitened = FALSE.


2. Three workable measurement models

A. Likelihood-only coefficients in a modest source basis
Represent each region’s BOLD series using a prespecified, low-dimensional neural source basis passed through its learned HRF:
\[
y_r=G_r a_r+Z_r\xi_r+\varepsilon_r,
\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_r)=\Sigma_r.
\]
When \(G_r\) has full column rank (e.g., well-spaced trial impulses or low-dimensional epoch bases) and is fit via unpenalized GLS in whitened coordinates,
\[
\widehat a_r=A_r y_r,\qquad A_rG_r=I,
\qquad E(\widehat a_r\mid a_r)=a_r,
\qquad \Omega_{rr}=A_r\Sigma_r A_r^{\top},
\qquad \Omega_{st}=A_s\Sigma_{\varepsilon_s,\varepsilon_t}A_t^{\top}.
\]
This provides an exact unbiased additive measurement-error model (\(K_r = I\)), closely paralleling likelihood-only coefficient reconstruction in REPAIR (Abdulrahman & Henson, 2016). In likelihood_only_bridge.R (16 source amplitudes, 180 BOLD volumes, distinct regional HRFs, shared/serial AR noise), source operators satisfy \(AG = I\) to 8.88e-16, and a 10,000-draw Monte Carlo check matches analytical source SDs within 1.5%. Its trade-off is design conditioning: rapid jittered event schedules or omitted sustained activity can make unpenalized \(G_r\) collinear or misspecified.


B. De-penalize only identifiable contrasts
For a linear Gaussian posterior with precision \(C_{\rm post}^{-1} = J + P_{\rm prior}\), likelihood information \(J\) is recoverable only on subspaces where \(J\) is well-conditioned. In likelihood_only_bridge.R, the full 180-column continuous convolution matrix has numerical rank 178, confirming why continuous TR-grid deconvolution cannot simply drop its penalty globally without projecting onto identifiable trial/window contrasts first.


C. Retain resolution \(K_s, K_t\) inside a joint latent Gaussian model
When unshrinking is ill-conditioned, \(K_s\) and \(K_t\) can be retained explicitly inside a joint Gaussian marginal likelihood over \((\widehat a_{s,g}, \widehat a_{t,g}) \mid z_g\). In joint_gaussian_demo.R (known unequal \(K_s \neq K_t\) and known \(\Omega\)), maximum likelihood recovered connectivity 0.507 (truth 0.550) and PPI 0.336 (truth 0.350) with a positive-definite Hessian, trading stronger distributional assumptions and computation for exact handling of non-identity resolution.


Gaussian conditional-mean calibration variant

Let \(m_s = E(a_s \mid \widehat a_s, z)\) under a Gaussian seed prior. With independent regional errors, \[
E(\widehat a_t \mid \widehat a_s, z) = K_t\{Z\gamma + \beta m_s + \delta\operatorname{diag}(z)m_s\},
\] requiring design columns \(K_t m_s\) and \(K_t \operatorname{diag}(z) m_s\) rather than multiplying \(m_s\) by \(z\) after applying \(K_t\), plus an explicit shared-noise regression term \(\Omega_{ts}(K_s V_s K_s^\top + \Omega_{ss})^{-1}(\widehat a_s - K_s \mu_s)\) whenever \(\Omega_{ts} \neq 0\).




3. Full cross-trial corrected-score estimating equations
For unbiased source measurements (\(K_s = K_t = I\)), form participant \(g\)’s centered trial design \(\widehat D_g = D_g + U_g\) for columns \([a_s,\, z,\, a_s z]\) and define full cross-trial error moments \(C_g = E(U_g^\top U_g)\) and \(c_g = E(U_g^\top v_g)\) (including run-centering projections applied consistently to both data and \(\Omega_{ss}, \Omega_{st}\)). Solving the summed participant corrected score (Nakamura, 1990; Buonaccorsi, 1996):
\[
q_g(\theta)=\widehat D_g^{\top}\widehat y_g-c_g
       -(\widehat D_g^{\top}\widehat D_g-C_g)\theta,
\qquad \sum_{g=1}^G q_g(\widehat\theta)=0,
\]
yields an unbiased estimating equation \(E[q_g(\theta_0)] = 0\) with participant-cluster sandwich variance:
\[
\widehat V=H^{-1}\left[\frac{G}{G-1}\sum_{g=1}^G
q_g(\widehat\theta)q_g(\widehat\theta)^{\top}\right]H^{-\top},
\quad
H=\sum_{g=1}^G(\widehat D_g^{\top}\widehat D_g-C_g).
\]


Prototype interface (measurement_error_models.R)

source("measurement_error_models.R")
fit <- fit_corrected(blocks, mode = "full")
stopifnot(fit$ok)
fit$estimate  # neural association, task main effect, PPI
fit$se        # participant-cluster score SEs
The prototype refuses indefinite corrected information matrices rather than silently regularizing unidentified designs.



4. Conditional simulation benchmarks (400 repetitions per scenario)
Each scenario simulates 400 repetitions of \(G = 60\) participants (Few participants uses \(G = 12\)) with 24 trials per participant, true connectivity \(\beta = 0.55\), task main effect \(\gamma = 0.25\), and PPI \(\delta = 0.35\) (Null sets \(\beta = \delta = 0\)), under serial trial error correlation \(0.55\) and shared cross-region error correlation \(0.45\).






Figure 10.1: Mean coefficient bias across three stress scenarios. Bars show plus/minus 1.96 Monte Carlo SE; horizontal scales differ across columns. The oracle uses true neural amplitudes. Empty Undo K rows mean that method was only evaluated in the unequal-resolution scenario.









Figure 10.2: Coverage of nominal 95% normal intervals. Bars are exact binomial 95% intervals for the Monte Carlo coverage probability, not individual-model confidence intervals. The dashed reference is 95%; all horizontal axes span 0–100%. Full + row SE and Full + cluster SE have the same point estimate.

Three practical lessons bridge these benchmarks back to empirical medusa analyses:

Omitting shared cross-parcel error creates severe false connectivity: Under Null serial + shared, ignoring \(\Omega_{st}\) (Zero shared covariance) falsely rejects in 95.0% of repetitions, whereas subtracting \(\Omega_{st}\) drops connectivity false positives to 5.0%—directly motivating shared_error = "auto" in Step 6.
Unequal source resolution requires matched HRF/inverse scales: When two parcels have markedly different effective smoothing (\(K_s \neq K_t\)), naive attenuation and resolution distortion can partially cancel (0.579) while variance-only disattenuation overshoots (0.767). Keep regularization policies matched across seed and target parcels and control shared task main effects carefully (Cole et al., 2019).
Small-\(G\) cohorts require finite-sample \(t\)/HKSJ adjustments: Normal asymptotic cluster SEs undercover at \(G = 12\) (MacKinnon, Nielsen & Webb, 2022), which is why decon_connectivity_repair() uses HKSJ \(t\)-intervals over participant slopes rather than normal row or unadjusted cluster \(z\)-intervals.

Designing a Study-Specific Calibration Check
The standalone medusa package is evaluated through two complementary layers of evidence:
Keeping the scope of each test distinct is essential: an algebraic check verifies that operator covariance propagation is exact conditional on a fitted noise model, whereas a Monte Carlo study measures bias and interval coverage under its specific data-generating process.
Before making high-stakes inferential claims on a novel task schedule—especially rapid event-related designs with variable-duration phases or trial-level PPI—run a compact synthetic calibration tailored to your exact study geometry:
crumbs: 11  Validation and the limits of the evidence

title: Validation and the limits of the evidence
text:
Lock the estimand and multiplicity family upfront: Prespecify the target parcels, peri-event lag grid, behavioral covariates, planned time windows, and study-wide adjustment rule ("holm" or "BY") before inspecting empirical \(p\)-values.
Use your actual empirical event schedule and censor masks: Simulate BOLD on the exact empirical onset times, reaction-time durations, run lengths, and framewise-displacement censor masks (valid_rows) from your cohort so collinearity and edge truncation match your real data.
Simulate both active signals and realistic structured nulls: Include voxelwise HRF variation across the physiological manifold, AR(\(p\)) temporal noise, spatially correlated parcel innovations, and—for Step 6 PPI—a stress null where shared physiological/motion noise varies across task conditions while true neural modulation is zero.
Refit the complete pipeline inside every Monte Carlo replicate: Keep Step 1 HRF/noise learning, Step 2 lambda and rwls = "auto" estimation, Step 3/4 epoch demixing and parcel weighting, and Step 5/6 inference inside the loop rather than freezing oracle operators.
Report bias, 95% CI coverage, null rejection, and convergence health together: Track missing edge-lag participants, isSingular() rates in mixed_by(), step-up regularization triggers in decon_connectivity_repair(), and binomial Monte Carlo intervals around empirical rejection and coverage rates.

title: Calibration of multi-lag trajectory inference
text:
Simulation Design
Step 5 introduced medusa_multilag_infer() for joint peri-event trajectory estimation, simultaneous confidence bands, 1D TFCE, epoch omnibus testing, and planned window contrasts. This chapter evaluates the empirical Type I error and 95% confidence-band coverage of medusa::medusa_multilag_infer() across 180 independent synthetic cohorts per scenario, separating two distinct error-rate targets:
Each Monte Carlo replication simulates 20 participants, 2 runs per participant, 6 peri-event lags (0 to 5 s), 1 active parcel, and 2 null parcels (Null A and Null B):
Note what this benchmark isolates: it starts at the participant trial panel to test group pooling, available-case edge support, studentized Wishart null calibration, and study-wide Holm adjustment under known lag covariance and serial trial dependence. End-to-end HRF/deconvolution estimation is evaluated separately in the 14-study validation suite.
crumbs: 12  Calibration of multi-lag trajectory inference

title: Calibration of multi-lag trajectory inference
text:
Realistic heteroskedasticity and cross-lag/cross-parcel dependence: Inter-trial intervals jitter between 3 and 9 seconds; Run 2 has \(1.6\times\) the residual SD of Run 1; residuals share common cross-parcel noise and positive cross-lag autocorrelation; and true participant slopes vary randomly around the population trajectory in every parcel.
Two benchmark regimes (180 replications each):

Complete / independent trials: Complete lag support for all 20 participants and independent trial innovations within each run.
Gaps / serially dependent trials: Adds serial autocorrelation in both behavioral predictor and neural trial residuals, drops random subsets of trials within runs, and censors the final edge lag entirely in 3 of the 20 participants. Under medusa_multilag_infer()’s available-case cross-lag pooling, all 20 participants are retained at supported lags (0–4 s) while the 17 uncensored participants inform lag 5 s.

Inference settings: Each replication runs the panel pathway of medusa_multilag_infer() with trajectory_mode = "none", contrast_source = "unsmoothed", 799 studentized Wishart null draws per trajectory, and a planned late_minus_early contrast ([3, 4] s minus [0, 1] s).

Key findings from the rejection and coverage benchmarks

title: What Woolrich’s noise study contributes
text:
Executive summary: Woolrich, Ripley, Brady, and Smith (2001), Temporal Autocorrelation in Univariate Linear Modeling of FMRI Data (NeuroImage 14, 1370–1386, DOI 10.1006/nimg.2001.0931), highlights three principles that directly shape Step 1 of medusa: (1) separating task mean-model mismatch from residual autocorrelation, (2) regularizing temporal covariance across neighboring voxels without pooling signed BOLD responses, and (3) estimating noise correlation and marginal noise scale coherently so propagated readout covariance \(B\Sigma B^\top\) is well calibrated. At the same time, our live diagnostic benchmarks show why replacing MEDuSA’s REML AR(\(p\)) cascade with a raw-residual Tukey lag taper is not advantageous under high-rank event-related mean models.

What Woolrich et al. (2001) actually demonstrate
Woolrich et al. (2001) compare temporal autocorrelation estimators for univariate task-activation GLMs. Their FILM procedure estimates residual autocorrelation, stabilizes long-lag estimates with a Tukey cosine lag taper:
\[
\widehat r_T(\ell)=
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12\{1+\cos(\pi\ell/M)\}\widehat r(\ell),&0\le\ell<M,\\
0,&\ell\ge M,
\end{cases}
\]
borrows information locally within tissue types (SUSAN), and prewhitens both data and design. Two nuances matter when translating their findings to modern fast-TR event-related deconvolution:

Bandwidth scales with TR, not volume count: Fifteen lags spans 45 s at \(\text{TR} = 3\text{ s}\) (Woolrich’s primary acquisition) but only 9.75 s at \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\).
Projection distortion grows with design rank: After projecting out an \(m\)-column event/nuisance design \(X\) (\(M_X = I - P_X\)), raw OLS residuals have covariance \(\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top \neq \Sigma\). In rapid trial-wise designs where \(X\) carries dozens of free event columns, raw-residual sample autocorrelations acquire substantial negative projection bias that simple lag tapering does not undo.



How medusa implements—and extends—these principles



Principle
Implementation in medusa::fit_crossrun_decon()
Methodological role




Separate HRF shape mismatch from noise autocorrelation
Two-pass target-excluding REML noise refit: Pass 1 estimates initial noise under a canonical fallback HRF + free event amplitudes + temporal derivatives; once cross-run HRFs are selected out-of-sample, Pass 2 refits each run’s AR(\(p\)) noise model using the selected HRF while keeping HRF selection strictly frozen
Prevents unmodeled fast/slow vascular dispersion from spilling into residuals and pushing \(\widehat\rho\) to the upper boundary (0.90).


Regularize temporal covariance without projection bias
Pooled AR(1) profile REML on the exact residual subspace \(M_X\) + shrunk residual AR(\(q\)) Yule–Walker correction with projection-bias adjustment
Achieves low-variance spectral regularization while accounting analytically for degrees-of-freedom and projection loss from \(M_X\).


Borrow spatially without cancelling opposing task signals
Averages REML log-likelihood profiles across voxels within each spatial_groups parcel rather than averaging raw BOLD time series
Voxels with positive, negative, or null task responses contribute coherently to shared physiological noise estimation.


Estimate correlation and marginal scale coherently
hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd() computes leverage-standardized, Winsorized GLS residual scale under the post-selection HRF and AR(\(p\)) cascade, converting innovation SD to stationary marginal noise_sd
Eliminates mismatch between temporal whitening correlation \(\Sigma_{\rm cor}\) and marginal amplitude \(\sigma_{\rm obs}\) in propagated covariance \(\Omega = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 B \Sigma_{\rm cor} B^\top\).





Live benchmark 1: Separating HRF mismatch from temporal autocorrelation
Using the Step 1 simulation (3 runs, \(\text{TR} = 0.65\text{ s}\), 360 volumes, 24 jittered events/run, 8 voxels each in Fast, Slow, and Null parcels, true noise parameters \(\rho = 0.65, \psi_1 = 0.20, \psi_2 = -0.30\)), we compare:

Canonical_HRF: Single-pass AR(\(p\)) noise estimation locked to a fixed canonical HRF (no post-selection refit).
Current_MEDuSA: Live fit_crossrun_decon() with its 2-pass post-selection REML AR(\(p\)) refit (using the out-of-sample cross-run selected HRF, zero target-run leakage).
Oracle_true_HRF: Noise fit conditioned on the exact data-generating HRF.
Tukey10/15/28 comparators: Pooled raw-residual Tukey lag tapers (\(M \in \{10, 15, 28\}\)) under either canonical or selected-HRF mean models.

Current MEDuSA (2-pass post-selection REML refit) overlaps the true generating ACF and Oracle HRF fit, whereas locking the mean model to a misspecified Canonical HRF inflates long-lag correlation, and raw-residual Tukey tapers exhibit projection distortion.


Two results stand out clearly:

Post-selection noise refitting eliminates HRF-induced autocorrelation inflation: Under a misspecified Canonical_HRF, unmodeled vascular shape residuals drive \(\widehat\rho\) to its upper bound in both active parcels (acf_RMSE_1_24 = 0.260 in Fast, 0.314 in Slow). Current_MEDuSA’s target-excluding 2-pass refit drops ACF RMSE to 0.006 (Fast) and 0.008 (Slow)—matching Oracle_true_HRF (0.006 and 0.008) without touching target-run HRF selection!
REML subspace likelihood outperforms raw-residual lag tapering: Even when given the selected HRF (Tukey15_selected), raw-residual Tukey tapering retains 0.090–0.100 ACF RMSE—even on the pure Null parcel (0.100 vs. 0.011 for Current_MEDuSA)—because projecting 24 free trial predictors + drift terms out of 360 volumes distorts sample residual autocorrelations (\(\operatorname{Cov}(r) = M_X \Sigma M_X^\top\)).



Live benchmark 2: Coherent marginal scale and propagated readout covariance
What ultimately matters for Step 3–6 inference is not the ACF plot in isolation, but the accuracy of the propagated trial readout covariance \(\Omega = \sigma_{\rm obs}^2 B \Sigma_{\rm cor} B^\top\). Evaluating a frozen linear inverse (\(\lambda = 0.01\), second-difference penalty) at event onsets, we compare Canonical_HRF vs. Current_MEDuSA under both the standalone second-difference scale (d2, estimate_decon_noise_sd()) and MEDuSA’s covariance-consistent GLS residual scale (gls, hrf_estimate_gls_noise_sd()). Notice how Canonical_HRF suffers from compensating errors that mask off-diagonal miscalibration: its overly persistent correlation matrix alone underestimates readout SEs by roughly half (SE / true (known SD) = 0.48–0.56), while unmodeled HRF residuals inflate its marginal SD by more than \(2\times\) (GLS SD / true = 2.04–2.28), leaving diagonal SEs near 1.10–1.14 even though the full trial-by-trial covariance matrix has 21–28% Frobenius error! Remaining frontiers and practical takeaways

Keep HRF groups tissue-homogeneous: In fit_crossrun_decon(), spatial_groups currently defines both HRF evidence pooling and AR(\(p\)) noise pooling. Avoid lumping high-pulsatility CSF/vascular-rim voxels into cortical gray-matter parcels; local tissue-aware noise neighborhoods (Parlak et al., 2023; Olszowy et al., 2019) remain a natural future refinement.
Match ar_order to acquisition TR: Default ar_order = "auto" (up to cascaded AR(3)) works well for standard and moderate multiband TRs (\(0.65\text{–}2.0\text{ s}\)); ultra-fast TRs (\(< 0.5\text{ s}\)) with unmodeled cardiac/respiratory aliases should pair physiological regressors (nuisance_list) with residual ACF inspection.
Remember what temporal prewhitening does not identify: Temporal whitening within each parcel calibrates \(\Omega_{rr}\), not cross-parcel shared noise \(\Omega_{st}\)—which is why fit_crossrun_decon() also retains task-free noise_innovations so Step 4 and Step 6 (shared_error = "auto") can estimate spatial noise covariance directly.

Kernel quadrature onto peri-event lag grids, collateral non-target removal (demix_other_events), post-readout ridge target demixing (demix_target_trials), within-trial lag demixing (demix_within_trial), duration "rate" vs. "integral" readout, exact Toeplitz error propagation (se_demixed), and fast C++ matrix-native descriptive alignment (align_medusa_ts()).
